item.title: What happened in F1 Mexican GP final practice
item.author: Jack Cozens
item.content:encoded: Lando Norris and Kimi Antonelli were near-inseparable in final practice for Formula 1's Mexican Grand Prix as Ferrari's pace faltered ahead of qualifying.Friday pacesetter Charles Leclerc ultimately ended up third for Ferrari, but only at the end of the session following aborted attempts at his qualifying simulation on soft tyres.He and team-mate Lewis Hamilton - whose session played out in a similar way - had traded fastest times at the beginning of FP3 as the top teams all chose to start the session on medium tyres.Mercedes was among the first of the frontrunners to switch to softs and while George Russell pondered whether a double-prep lap was necessary, telling the team to consider telling Antonelli to push after a single warm-up lap, Antonelli did complete two prep laps and duly went fastest with a 1m17.601s.That looked as though it would stand as the session's best time until Norris improved with two minutes left of the hour-long session, going one thousandth quicker for McLaren.Leclerc was 0.117s back in third, suggesting the Ferrari will remain a contender for pole in qualifying, while Oscar Piastri ended the session within two tenths of his pacesetting McLaren team-mate in fourth.Max Verstappen complained of brake issues late on and was three and a half tenths down in fifth ahead of Hamilton, with less than seven hundredths covering the Ferrari in sixth and Arvid Lindblad at the back of the top 10, as Racing Bulls again had both drivers inside the theoretical Q3 cutoff.Lindblad and ninth-fastest Lawson were well clear of their midfield rivals, with Nico Hulkenberg four tenths further back for Audi ahead of Alpine duo Franco Colapinto and Pierre Gasly and Fernando Alonso's Aston Martin.Hulkenberg set the joint-highest number of laps in the session (32) alongside Ryo Hirakawa, parachuted in to the second Haas seat for the remainder of the weekend with Esteban Ocon replaced ahead of FP3.Hirakawa ran through a full programme including plenty of opportunities for single push laps, and by the end of a session where he used three sets of softs had a best time of 1m19.504s that left him 19th, 1.904s off the pace and inside six tenths of team-mate Ollie Bearman.Home driver Sergio Perez was one of two drivers, alongside Audi's Gabriel Bortoleto, who failed to set a time.Perez completed just one installation lap before returning to the Cadillac garage, where the team opted to make a precautionary engine change before qualifying.His team-mate Valtteri Bottas was 20th, 2.742s off the pace and 0.838s behind Hirakawa.1 item.title: Canadian Cyclo-cross National Championships: Sidney McGill wins elite women's title
item.author: Lyne Lamoureux
item.content:encoded: Sidney McGill (Materiaal-Lastig) claimed her first elite Canadian women’s cyclocross title with a commanding solo victory at the 2026 Lazer Canadian Cyclocross Championships in Oro-Medonte, Ontario. The 27-year-old, who previously won the elite Pan American title in Missoula in 2024, reached the top step after finishing second and third in the previous two editions. McGill dominated the race, crossing the finish line with a lead of more than four minutes.McGill started her cyclo-cross season by taking three UCI victories and finishing on the podium of all but one of 11 UCI races. Sarina Daigle (Passion Project) crossed the line 4:39 later to take silver, while Siobhan Kelly (Black Dog Racing) followed two minutes later to round out the podium.Last year’s winner, four-time national champion Maghalie Rochette, was absent from the race as she is expecting a baby.Nico Knoll took a solo victory to win the Under-23 title crossing the line 48 seconds ahead of her closest rivals. In a battle with her Caledon Hills Armada teammate, Aislin Hallahan claimed the silver ahead of bronze medallist Eli Clark.Earlier in the day, Alexa Haviland (Shredders Race Team) claimed the women's junior title with a solo victory, finishing 76 seconds ahead of silver medallist Anna Christensen (Shredders Race Team). Claire MacKinnon (Stimulus Trek Racing Team) rounded out the podium in third.Held at Hardwood Ski and Bike, a four-season outdoor recreation centre just north of Barrie, Ontario, the race featured an approximately 3km course that challenged riders with natural obstacles, sandy sections, tight corners, and steep run-up climbs.The road season might be at an end, but Cyclingnews isn't slowing down. item.title: Hadjar escapes with warning for pushing Mexico F1 paddock guest
item.author: Jack Cozens
item.content:encoded: Isack Hadjar has been given a formal warning for pushing a guest in the paddock ahead of the first Formula 1 practice session at the Mexican Grand Prix.Footage circulated on social media on Friday that appeared to show Hadjar pushing someone who had tried to take a selfie with him.The Red Bull driver was subsequently called to see the F1 stewards on Saturday morning for what the summons document described as 'alleged misconduct'.Hadjar stated in his appearance in front of the stewards that he was running late for FP1 and, having stopped for a photograph with a young fan, was "approached by a paddock guest in an aggressive manner".The stewards' document detailing that account also said "one security person was walking behind him [Hadjar] and was unable tointervene and prevent what was tantamount to an invasion of the driver's private space".Having initially resisted that move, Hadjar subsequently "pushed him aside with his open right hand" - a breach of article 12.2.1.l of the FIA international sporting code relating to misconduct.However, in awarding only a warning the stewards acknowledge five mitigating circumstances in Hadjar's favour, in line with the guidelines in appendix B of the ISC.These were that Hadjar was "reacting to an uninvited and rather aggressive action by another person"; that he was trying to make his way to the Red Bull garage for FP1 through a congested area; that he did not have "sufficient" security present; that the guest invaded his personal space without consent; and the "general issue" drivers have moving through the paddock.

item.title: Yankees Arizona Fall League Week 4 Recap
item.author: Michael Zeno
item.content:encoded: We’re heading down the stretch in Arizona, as less than two weeks remain in the regular season for the six teams playing in the desert. The Salt River Rafters have fallen to 11-10 after a hot start and seem doomed to have to get through the postseason the hard way, but there’s still plenty of time to fix that. They’ll need the Yankees’ contingent to be a big part of it; they had an up-and-down week headlined by some titanic tanks from Kyle West. As a reminder, if you want a quick rundown on who’s in the desert this month, check here.October 24 (Rafters 3, Saguaros 5): The Rafters started the week with a sluggish, seven-inning loss that was shut out until pretty late. Dax Kilby got things started by going 2-for-4 with a pair of singles and a stolen base. On the mound, JT Etheridge struggled with command, allowing two runs on four walks in three innings. Mack Estrada worked around a pair of walks in a scoreless fourth, as did Antonio Gomez in the fifth, as he got his fastball up to 98. The highlight of this game was West, who annihilated his first home run of the spring at 111.9 mph and 409 feet late in the game.October 26 (Rafters 20, Saguaros 4): Do you think Salt River was angry about how the game on Saturday went? They put up a staggering 20 runs in a blowout on Monday, partially from the Yankees’ contingent. Core Jackson went 0-for-5 with a walk, RBI, and four strikeouts; Anthony Mena tossed a pair of scoreless innings late in the blowout, but the star was once again West. He pummeled a pair of home runs a combined 912 feet. He ended the day with three hits, two homers, a double, and four RBIs with exit velocities of 112.0, 109.2, and 100.4.October 27 (Rafters 0, Desert Dogs 1): One day after scoring 20, the Rafters were shut out across nine innings. That’s baseball, Suzyn! Kilby went 0-f0r-4 and Chris Veach tossed two scoreless innings to continue a strong month down in the desert. Not much going on here.October 28 (Rafters 4, Scorpions 0): A second straight day of strong pitching vaulted Salt River to a shutout victory on Wednesday. Kilby went 1-for-3 with two walks and a few hard-hit balls, including a roped 107.9 mph single. Jackson went 0-for-2 with a walk and a strikeout, West went 0-for-4 with two strikeouts, and Gomez had his best day in a while on the mound, striking out two in a scoreless inning. His velocity was a lot more stable around 98 and generated a lot of called strikes.October 29 (Rafters 5, Solar Sox 21): Ouch. Not a great way to finish the week, especially after the games were cancelled on Friday. Fortunately, the Yankees weren’t really at fault. Kilby tripled twice, including with a 109.3 mph, 409-foot booming shot off the wall in center field. He did make a pair of errors at shortstop in an ugly game for Salt River’s defense that included one from West as well. In an ugly game for pitchers, Estrada didn’t allow a run in two-thirds of an inning. 17-53 (.304), 2 HR, 8 RBI, 6 2B, 3 3B, 6 BB, 7 K, 5 SB 5-40 (.125), HR, 3 RBI, 2B, 3B, 14 BB, 16 K, 10 SB 11-46 (.239), 3 HR, 10 RBI, 2B, 7 BB, 11 K, 3 SB9 IP, 7 H, 6 R (5 ER), 7 BB, 13 K5.2 IP, 2 H, 1 R, 7 BB, 2 K9.2 IP, 5 H, 4 R, 4 BB, 12 K 9.2 IP, 9 H, 4 R (3 ER), 5 BB, 7 K 5.1 IP, 7 H, 5 R, 6 BB, 5 K

item.title: Tadej Pogačar reveals three fractured vertebrae after Vuelta crash: “I’m just happy to be alive”
item.author: Lyne Lamoureux
item.content:encoded: Tadej Pogačar revealed that his injuries sustained in his crash at the Vuelta a España were more extensive than first reported. Initial reports stated that the five-time Tour de France winner had suffered a concussion, fractures to his left collarbone, a stable C7 cervical fracture as well as various cuts and bruises. But weeks after his crash, further exams showed that he had broken two more vertebrae.“There’s actually a funny story,” Pogačar began the interview with . “Two weeks ago, I was in Slovenia and I went to do another CT scan. I knew I had a C7 fracture, but then we saw I had two more broken vertebrae, the T1 and T2.”“At that moment, I was happy I didn’t do the European Championships, which had been my initial goal. When I saw I had three broken vertebrae? I’m just happy to be alive, actually, or just to be standing.”He added that he has largely returned to his normal routine, although he is still taking precautions as he continues his recovery.“I don’t have discomfort anymore,” Pogačar said. “I have to be careful not to crash on the bike, or do some heavy lifting with my left arm or with my neck. But I can do basically everything normal now.”The UAE Team Emirates rider admitted that the two weeks post-crash were difficult, with concussion-related nausea and dizziness affecting his coordination and forcing a delay in getting back onto his bike, or at a minimum, on the rollers.“For the first two weeks, I was really mentally not OK. I was really down. I was not a fun person to be around. I don’t think Urska [Zigart] was happy to see me around the house, because I was just, like, depressed. You know, just not feeling anything.”Everything changed once he got back into training.“When I started to get on the home trainer, to go to physio every day, then I started to feel better — also in the head. But it was a day-to-day fight.”“Now, in Monaco, I go for runs, swum a few times — it’s important to build a really good base now through the winter. Actually, it’s not winter yet here — I was in shorts today riding outside. But I‘m feeling like I’m getting back into the proper rhythm of training and recovery.”The road season might be at an end, but Cyclingnews isn't slowing down. item.title: All the reasons the Ocon-Haas relationship fell apart
item.author: Ben Anderson
item.content:encoded: Haas is staying tight-lipped, but its sudden decision to replace Esteban Ocon with Ryo Hirakawa at Formula 1's Mexican Grand Prix suggests its regular (and soon-to-be-former) driver has been benched.In this piece, first published at the end of September when Ocon's end-of-2026 exit was announced, Ben Anderson and Scott Mitchell-Malm look at how the move turned sour.Such comments inevitably lead to speculation over what is really behind the decision if not purely a choice based on driver performance.As Ferrari-backed Rafa Camara is the favourite to replace Ocon, some sympathetic to Ocon's cause have inferred that Ferrari's support of its junior driver is shoving Ocon out the door.There have also been some suggestions of Haas prioritising a commercial element. And Ocon has his own detractors too, those who believe he has simply not been good enough after being outscored by team-mate Ollie Bearman over the two years.Haas had a contractual option to retain Ocon for next year and decided not to activate it quite a long time ago, subsequently notifying Ocon just after the summer break that he was unlikely to be kept on.It has been a significant shift since Ocon being so highly coveted by Haas. When Ocon was signed, team boss Ayao Komatsu was faced with a lot of questions about whether it would work, though there could be no doubt about Ocon's pedigree coming in.Not since 10-time podium finisher Romain Grosjean joined for the team's inaugural F1 season in 2016 as Haas employed such a successful driver.He also arrived carrying the label of sometimes being a difficult driver to work with, who had clashed with team-mates multiple times, and joined after being dropped by Alpine before the final race of 2024 and replaced with Jack Doohan. And was known to disagree with his past teams over the extent of perceived car issues he said were holding him back.It's also worth remembering that Mercedes ultimately decided Ocon wasn't quite good enough to warrant replacing Valtteri Bottas in the way George Russell ultimately did.Komatsu was still willing to gamble. It just did not pay off as hoped.Komatsu, who pushed hard to bring Ocon to the team, felt their previous relationship dating back to Komatsu's time as a senior engineer at what's now Alpine during its Lotus era, when Ocon was a member of the Lotus F1 junior team (pictured together in 2014 below) before Mercedes snapped him up, would help smooth things along and prevent any tensions that arose spilling over.In one specific aspect this has been a success: Ocon and team-mate Bearman have maintained a good working relationship throughout Ocon's spell with the team, and even when there have been flashpoints, such as a collision at the 2025 British Grand Prix and another at Spa this year, those moments have been addressed internally and fostered no ill-will between the two drivers.What Komatsu misjudged is how well it would work more broadly. He was fully aware that Ocon had some difficult moments, but put that down to Alpine handling him poorly as that team was going through frequent turmoil and upheaval during its transition from the Cyril Abiteboul regime Ocon began with, to the Flavio Briatore-led one that ousted him.Haas had to work hard in the early part of 2025 to push past the mental baggage Ocon carried from how he felt he was mistreated during the final races of his Alpine stint, as that team coalesced around Pierre Gasly and edged Ocon toward the exit.But the team began to notice a worrying pattern: when results didn't go Ocon's way he would become defensive and tensions in the garage would rise and Haas gradually felt there was ultimately a lack of accountability for his own issues.This is not a problem unique to Ocon. Many drivers get trapped in a paranoid mindset and it's worth remembering the specific background to Ocon's racing career. He got to F1 against all financial odds, with absolutely no silver spoon in his mouth, overcoming adversity right from his earliest days in karting.So he was probably always more likely than most to have a 'me against the world' mentality. When you have to fight your way into F1 in the first place, that combative streak can be a very powerful weapon - but it can also become all too easily ingrained.As the defeats to Bearman piled up through the course of 2025, Ocon began repeating complaints publicly about his car, in particular the brakes. At the start of 2026 Haas made a concerted effort to get proper alignment between Ocon and all the staff working on his side of the garage.But as the year has gone on and Haas has slowly realised it has deeper technical issues itself to deal with, tensions have risen again.The team ultimately feels Ocon has been too combative internally when backs have been against the wall, as well as questioning car specifications or performance discrepancies, or wasting time on blind-alley set-up work.This is likely to be a matter of perspective. Ocon almost certainly believes he is just being straightforward, doing the job of trying to push the team forward by being demanding, as was mapped out right from the start - and therefore Haas is simply now using the thing they said they wanted from him originally against him.Why mini-revival hasn't saved himOcon has only occasionally shown the best of himself at Haas. Some excellent race results in his first year were overshadowed by a general qualifying struggle over the season and a particular, inconsistent problem pushing the car on the brakes in the final part of the year.This year, he missed the small window to score big results when Haas was more competitive before its form declined in the midfield - a mix of his own misjudgement like in China and some genuine misfortune with safety car timings.That has warped the points situation versus Bearman, who scored 17 of his 20 points in the first two races. Since then it's 7-3 in Ocon's favour. And he has been better than what some seem willing to credit him for.Haas's decline and the onset of more car inconsistencies - this time on both sides of the garage - have prevented Ocon from doing anything standout to plead his case. This has to be considered a degree of mitigation for Ocon. Bearman said it makes it “really challenging” for the drivers because the behaviour can change completely from track to track. Still, even a mini-revival hasn't changed Ocon's fate.His general performances and attitude did improvesince Haas told him his F1 career with the team was hanging by a thread. And had Ocon performed at the level he's shown since the end of the summer break consistently over the majority of the past 18 months, Haas would view the situation very differently. Ocon would have a strong case for being retained. Komatsu rates Ocon very highly when he's at his best, and also likes him as a person - feeling he is a genuinely nice guy when all is well and amicable. It's simply the case that Ocon's working relationship became strained and his time at Haas has been a cycle of short bursts of sustained improvement, followed by a regression to old bad habits.Taking Baku as an example, where Ocon qualified 13th but beat Bearman to eighth in the race, Haas was left unimpressed by the way Ocon reacted to his Q2 exit in qualifying, failing to take responsibility for an error on his first run then reacting badly to a yellow flag interruption on his second run that Bearman - who also went out in Q2 in the same circumstances - handled much better, despite being the younger and less experienced driver.Ocon also switched the running order of the cars without informing the team, seen as further evidence Ocon can sometimes act in his own interests rather than those of the team. Although by this time you could argue he knows he's on his way out - so why bother going the extra mile to keep Haas happy?Ocon's Baku race performance reminds everyone of the calibre of driver Ocon is and what he can bring at his best. But it was not simply a case of too littletoo late, just generally too late.Money factor is secondaryOther speculation has surrounded Haas's perceived financial uncertainty and claims that owner Gene Haas wants Camara because it will bring in necessary commercial backing.The eponymous team owner's position is said to be far less involved than that, though. He will just rubber-stamp whatever Komatsu decides or have the final say if there's a close call. There is not an indication that Haas himself is ordering this move or has even guided its direction.So, where might money have crept into it?The Race understands that Komatsu told Ocon he was unlikely to be retained in 2027 after the summer break, although it was not a definitive ‘you're out'.Haas felt that, on the balance of the results and performance levels Ocon had delivered so far, it couldn't justify paying him what is understood to be a multi-million dollar salary.It's fair to wonder how much of this is purely driven by Ocon failing to justify the money Haas is paying him, and how much is down to the commercial reality of Haas operating below the cost cap and generally being underfunded.And it's possible that Ocon took this as the team not being willing to pay for a driver of his track record, hence his remarks about there being elements at play behind the scenes that are “out of my control”.Money was at least a secondary factor in who should replace him. Komatsu has admitted that if two drivers were of equal perceived performance then “affiliations or the packages they've got matters”.There is an understanding that Camara's arrival will come with commercial benefits from South America that Ocon himself cannot match. That's undeniably to Haas's benefit that Camara comes with a big commercial benefit - from his personal Brazilian backers, rather than Ferrari - but the package he offers is not thought to be at the scale Haas title sponsor Toyota could bring to get current test driver Ryo Hirakawa that seat, for example.If Haas was purely prioritising money/marketing reasons over competitive considerations, Hirakawa would be the obvious choice here.But it was agreed he would only get the nod if he was also fastest in the shootout. He wasn't. Toyota knows this and has accepted it.The prospect of Camara lining up alongside Bearman - long considered a future Ferrari driver and a long-time protege - has caused some to draw unfair comparisons to Red Bull controlling two teams' driver line-ups in F1.Haas is not a Ferrari-controlled vehicle for it to just test junior drivers. The affiliation affords access and makes it a lot more convenient, so it greases the wheels certainly. But there is no prerequisite and nothing Ferrari can do to force Haas to take a driver it does not want. In that sense, Haas likely having an all-Ferrari pairing has been described to The Race as more of a ‘coincidence' than anything else. Ocon was never going to be retained over Bearman, considering Bearman's Ferrari support, age, and higher potential, as well as his Max Verstappen-esque tolerance for rear instability in the car.So, with Bearman set to stay, Ocon had to ward off these external threats to earn his own seat. As these alternatives pressed their case during various Testing Of Previous Cars evaluations, so Haas realised: why pay Ocon for a job they felt, over a season, someone else could do - and potentially do better - without the baggage and hassle following the incumbent driver around?The emergence of Camara sealed the deal. Haas tested him at Portimao and was blown away by Camara's immense one-lap pace - so strong that, on the day, even Bearman couldn't match him with the reference work he did.That's not to suggest Camara is quicker than Bearman overall, but it basically serves as evidence that on the shootout day Camara was the standout. Hirakawa came in second best, while McLaren junior Leonardo Fornaroli was fast in steady state conditions but struggled when things became windier and trickier.Ally that to the professional and focused attitude Camara displayed throughout proceedings, and it was in the end an easy decision for Haas to make - especially once it had decided that Ocon's time at the team needed to come to an end.

item.title: A world-first focus on long-term outcomes could transform UK government – or create new spending fights
item.author: Peter Walker Senior political correspondent
item.content:encoded: Tucked away in John Healey’s budget is decision to ringfence preventative projects where future savings outweigh initial costIt merited the briefest of mentions in John Healey’s speech and just one paragraph in the 166-page budget document, but some believe it could revolutionise not just public spending but the very process of government itself: a new focus on long-term outcomes.The idea in the broad sense is very simple. Any spending deemed to be “preventative” – that is, the initial outlay will be more than made up for by future savings – will from now on be ringfenced, meaning it cannot be raided for more immediate needs.Continue reading...

item.content:encoded: Legal experts welcome judge’s rejection of firing of James Comey’s daughter prosecutor but warn an appeal is likelyA recent legal ruling against an effort to fire the star-prosecutor daughter of a former FBI chief targeted by Donald Trump could send a strong message about politicized firings – and influence other judges weighing similar cases, legal veterans said.Judge Jesse Furman ruled this week that the Department of Justice’s firing of assistant US attorney Maurene Comey without cause was unlawful. Comey, the daughter of former FBI director James Comey, successfully litigated numerous high-profile cases during her tenure at the southern district of New York, including guilty verdicts against Ghislaine Maxwell and Sean “Diddy” Combs.Continue reading...

item.title: Best Buy is bundling a $100 gift card with touchscreen MacBook Pro preorders
item.author: Brad Bourque
item.content:encoded: While the new touch-enabled MacBook Pro with the PROLED XDR screen is available for preorder across a few major retailers, Best Buy is sweetening the deal by including a $100 gift card. The gift card will be automatically added to your cart when you preorder one of Apple’s highest-end laptops available in 14- or 16-inch configurations, and even one of its 14-inch MacBook Pro laptops with the M6 chip. You can verify that it’s been added to your order in the “Complete your purchase” section of the checkout page.My colleague Antonio G. Di Benedetto got a chance to check out the new laptop at Apple’s event, and came away impressed by the Tandem OLED panel’s brightness and contrast, but described the update as “kind of boring” given the relatively small changes to the system otherwise. There are some unique changes to macOS that help make the new touch experience smoother, like magnifying the traffic light-colored buttons on windows when you move your finger near them. The PROLED laptops are also a bit thinner and lighter than standard models, and the Apple logo on the back glows like on older versions.

item.title: Ocon suddenly replaced at Haas for rest of Mexico F1 weekend
item.author: Josh Suttill
item.content:encoded: Esteban Ocon will sit out the rest of Formula 1's Mexican Grand Prix with Haas reserve driver Ryo Hirakawa replacing him.Haas unexpectedly released a short statement on Saturday morning announcing the switch."TGR Haas F1 team reserve driver Ryo Hirakawa will replace Esteban Ocon for the remainder of the weekend's Mexico City Grand Prix," the statement read."Hirakawa, a two-time winner of the FIA World Endurance Championship and 24 Hours of Le Mans Winner with Toyota Gazoo Racing, participated in FP1 at the Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez on Friday 30 October - his third free practice outing of the season driving the VF-26, finishing 15th overall."The Japanese driver will partner team-mate Ollie Bearman through final practice and qualifying on Saturday and Sunday's 71-lap grand prix - Hirakawa's Formula 1 race debut."No further statements will be made at this time."No reason has been given for the change but Haas has confirmed it is not due to illness for Ocon.It is logical therefore to reason that he appears to have been benched.Ocon had a frustrating Friday in Mexico, publicly expressing his dissatisfaction with his runplan in FP2 - his only session in the car, after 32-year-old Hirakawa drove in FP1 to satisfy the rookie practice rule.His time was not bad - after getting the car back off Hirakawa for FP2, Ocon beat team-mate Ollie Bearman to end up a respectable 13th - but there was friction on the radio with his engineer Laura Mueller.: We've swapped the high fuel run to medium because Ollie's [tyre] appearance is not great.: Still doing soft, right?: No, we have to do medium.: No, no, I wanted the soft, like, don't do that to me. Come on.Ocon was visibly dissatisfied in the paddock after the session, keeping his helmet on as he returned to Haas's hospitality unit.Camara beat the likes of Toyota-backed driver Hirakawa to secure the seat.Two-time WEC champion Hirakawa has completed multiple F1 practice outings for McLaren, Alpine and Haas since the end of 2024, with a long-stated aim of racing in F1.The team is making no comment on its driver line-up for the next race in Brazil, in keeping with its statement.

item.title: What has haunted the Yankees in the 2020s?
item.author: John Griffin
item.content:encoded: Ah, Halloween. On this glorious intersection of Allhallowtide and capitalist consumerism run rampant, we herald in the year’s final days by celebrating all things spooky, as we let ghouls, goblins, and children dressed up in overpriced costumes run wild in one last day and night of outdoor tomfoolery before the cold darkness of a lockout-lengthened winter sets in.In the spirit of this haunting-filled day, let’s look back at the last few years. While, perhaps understandably, we tend to focus on the Yankees’ recent history, many of the decisions made over the last couple of years have been influenced by actions — or the lack of action — taken by the team as long ago as a decade. Which moves have haunted the Bronx the most in recent years? Let’s take a trip down memory lane.To some extent, everything comes back to the 2018-19 offseason, when Manny Machado and Bryce Harper were free agents. Following a year in which the Yankees won 100 games but were absolutely shellacked by the eventual champion Red Sox team. That Bombers team had an aging Brett Gardner in left, Didi Gregorius out for months due to a torn UCL, and a ton of uncertainty in the infield — Luke Voit’s breakout was fun, but there’s always reason to be wary of an age-27 breakout at first base; meanwhile, a young Gleyber Torres and Miguel Andujar had finished second and third in the AL Rookie of the Year voting, but there was reason to skeptical of Andujar’s performance at the plate and his ability to stick at third long-term. In short: the Yankees were good, but not so good that they couldn’t benefit from adding a superstar in his age-26 season, and lo and behold, not only were there two of them out there on the market, both were interested in donning the pinstripes — and Harper was supposedly even willing to learn first base to do it.So naturally, the Yankees prioritized getting under the luxury tax, and well, since then, they’ve had problem after problem that could’ve been solved by literally having paid one of these two guys — especially Machado. Concerns about Andujar turned out to be warranted, and then he tore his labrum. It’s only now as a part-time player over the past two years that he’s finally been able to carve out a role for himself. Gio Urshela was really good replacing him during the #NextManUp campaign, and followed that up with a solid 2020, but soon regressed into the journeyman utility player he had been. The Josh Donaldson experience? A disaster. DJ LeMahieu? The first contract worked, but he soon became always injured. Oswaldo Cabrera? Although a fun player, never more than a fill-in. Jazz Chisholm Jr.? A second baseman out of position. Ryan McMahon? Somehow a brief improvement before an ugly 2026. Sure, Machado’s contract is now a bit of an albatross, as he’s owed $39 million through 2033, but that’s the result of the extension the Padres signed him to, not the original deal.The biggest excuse given for not seriously pursuing Harper in 2018 was that he was an outfielder, and the Yankees had plenty of depth there. Well, Father Time came for Gardner, injuries caught up to Giancarlo Stanton and Clint Frazier, and Aaron Hicks experienced a severe and sudden decline. Since 2019, the Yankees have traded for Joey Gallo, Harrison Bader, Alex Verdugo, Juan Soto, Trent Grisham, Cody Bellinger, and Heliot Ramos in order to fix their outfield — and that doesn’t include the small army of players acquired simply to get injuries, such as Mike Tauchman and Jake Bauers, or the multiple prospects who have failed to stick. The team sure could’ve used Harper in any of those stretches … oh, and as it turns out, he’s a decent enough first baseman, too — yet another position that has been a bit of a revolving door.Sure, the Yankees may currently be fine at the first base/DH spot and have their corner outfield set, but let’s be real, each of the last few seasons has ended with Hal Steinbrenner on the podium saying the team needs to be more consistent at the plate, and either one of these two would have gone a long way towards remedying that problem.In the days following the 2014 season, the main question surrounding the Yankees was, “How are they going to replace the legendary Derek Jeter?” The solution, as it turned out, was rather easy: Didi Gregorius, a young shortstop acquired from the Arizona Diamondback as part of a three-way deal in exchange for Shane Greene. While it wasn’t quite as seamless as the DiMaggio-to-Mantle transition in the 1950s, Sir Didi went on to become a fan favorite — and, at least during the juiced ball era, a veritable middle-of-the-order bat.Unfortunately, once Gregorius’s years of team control ran out after the 2019 season, the Yankees embarked on a years-long merry-go-round trying to replace him. First, the team turned to former top prospect Gleyber Torres, who had performed admirably filling in at shortstop when Gregorius was injured but was clearly most comfortable at the keystone — something that was clear to anybody with eyes after the 2020 season; the team then had to keep him at short after re-signing LeMahieu instead of making a harder push for Francisco Lindor. When that, rather predictably, failed, the team had to use Urshela and the anonymous Andrew Velazquez there down the stretch in 2021.Rather than trying to sign Carlos Correa to the pillow contract he ended up getting from the Twins or making a play for future Rangers World Series MVP Corey Seager, the Yankees then swung a deal for Isiah Kiner-Falefa (not a bad player, miscast as a starting shortstop on a contender). When that went bust, they then handed the keys over to another top prospect who profiled more as a second baseman while in the minors, Anthony Volpe. The 22-year-old beat out fellow acclaimed up-and-comer Oswald Peraza, but neither were truly up for the job. Despite some stretches of time in which he looked to be taking the next step offensively — and a Gold Glove in what was admittedly a down year for AL shortstops — that ended as well as the Torres experiment. In the meantime, they opted not to pursue a shortstop in free agency, leaving them with no other options.Will George Lombard Jr. help get the Yankees out of their post-Gregorius cycle, and finally allow this ghost to reset? I’m hopeful, but it remains to be seen.The Devin Williams ConundrumOnce the Yankees signed Max Fried during the 2024-25 offseason, the rotation seemed to be a bit overflowing with arms, especially lefties. As such, the team decided to package Nestor Cortes with Caleb Durbin, a relatively minor infield prospect whose stock had risen during the 2024 season, and sent them both to the Brewers in exchange for arguably the best closer in baseball, Devin Williams. It was a move that, at the time, made sense: Clay Holmes was departing in free agency, the team needed another bullpen arm, and at the time, Nasty Nestor was behind Fried, Gerrit Cole, Carlos Rodón, Luis Gil, and Clarke Schmidt in the rotation pecking order.This move, though, has already had major consequences — and will continue to do so, for the foreseeable future. First, the injury bug hit the Yankees rotation hard in 2025: Cole missed the full season with a torn UCL, Schmidt was gone for the latter half, and Gil made just 11 starts. The team was forced to rely on Marcus Stroman, who they had tried to dump that winter, and Ryan Yarbrough, who was signed as a bullpen arm, for 17 starts (oh, and both of them also hit the shelf). If it wasn’t for Cam Schlittler’s breakout and the trio of Fried, Rodón, and a rookie Will Warren making 33 starts apiece, the season would’ve been a disaster; and while Cortes himself spent much of the year injured, the psychological part of trading away what would have been sorely-needed depth stung.To make matters worse, Durbin has developed into a solid third baseman with a league average bat, who finished top-three in the NL Rookie of the Year vote in 2025 before getting shipped to the Red Sox over the winter. Although he’s no superstar, his 4.4 rWAR/2.8 fWAR would have been miles better than the replacement-level play the Yankees got at the hot corner this season.Had Williams been a dominant closer, this would have been an OK pill to swallow. Except … he was easily the second-worst closer the Yankees have had in recent years, and probably the worst when you factor in only the performance on the field.The list of baseball-related things my Boston friends and I agree on is very short. Johnny Damon was fun to watch. The Mookie Betts trade was a disgrace. Aroldis Chapman sucks.Yea, that’s pretty much it. From a purely baseball perspective, the decision to trade for Chapman was great — the prospects the Yankees sent over didn’t really amount to anything. The decision to trade him to the Cubs was even better, as it introduced Gleyber to the Bronx and brought Adam Warren back where he belonged. The decision to sign him again that winter was…defensible, even if I didn’t exactly love the idea of spending big money on a reliever during what I expected to be a down year (remember, expectations heading into 2017 were ). So why does this move haunt the Yankees? Well, because I absolutely despise the fact that he ever donned the pinstripes, and hate the fact that, if I ever need to look up his stats on Baseball Reference after he retires, there’s a solid chance the site will use a picture of him in a Yankee uniform as his profile picture since his seven seasons in the Bronx represents—and will likely forever represent—his longest tenure with any one team.You’ll hear boos from more than just ghosts if you ever play that clip in the Bronx.

item.title: What F1 teams have done to tackle Mexico's altitude challenge
item.author: Gary Anderson
item.content:encoded: The Mexico City track is one of the outliers of the Formula 1 season, mainly because of the altitude: it is 2240 meters above sea level, which equates to roughly 25% less dense air, so it makes everything just that bit more difficult.For the drivers it's basically harder work, but for the cars it's a very different story, because at that altitude the cars will produce less downforce and with that less drag. In the past, teams would use more or less Monaco-specification wings but this season with the change in wing regulations and active aero they don't have that possibility.So, basically the ars will slide around more but the reduced drag means that top speeds are even faster than normal. This means that you will arrive at the end of those long straights faster and require a longer braking duration, which generates more heat in the brakes.These cars are turbocharged so in reality even though the turbo has to work harder and will be running at or as near to its maximum rpm as possible for most of the lap, it will still produce similar levels of power output. This means the engine's heat rejection isn't reduced, so you need to cool the cars roughly 25% more than you normally have to.Also, as it's an electrical energy-rich circuit layout you will also generate more heat into the battery pack and its control systems simply from harvesting and deployment.Basically, everything needs higher levels of cooling and below I have had a look at the top-four teams' changes from what they normally run. It's not easy to alter the inlet area on these cars as it is part of the side impact structure, so changing it would basically require redoing the side impact tests, so instead everyone will focus on the cooling exits, size, location and quantity.First of all we can have a look at the rear exits.The red ellipse highlights the rearwards-facing outlet. McLaren has raised the section above the exhaust outlet to increase the exit area.It already ran a spec-two outlet at Austin and as can be seen by the red ellipse Mercedes has retained that for Mexico. Now it is more of a triangular opening, which it has achieved by lifting the upper engine cover surface, especially in the central section, above the exhaust outlet.Ferrari has gone for simply a bigger exit at the sides, as highlighted by the two green ellipses. The central section is similar in height to the previous version.From what I can see, Red Bull hasn't really bothered to alter the outlet in this area.The rear exits are in more or less the same position and, in reality, are more or less the same size for all the teams - so the effect they have on the overall cars efficiency will be well understood.When you are getting the maximum from that area then it's onto the sidepod and engine-cover louvre outlets. This is the most critical area as far as maximising the cooling is concerned, and major changes in this area can affect the airflow structure of the rest of the car coming along behind. It's not just about bigger louvres, it's more about placement relative to the body-surface pressure and how and where those louvres are placed can have a major influence.The top two cars in this comparison, Mercedes and Ferrari, are fairly similar in placement and both have two fairly well-defined locations. These positions are normally placed where the internal radiator flow is at its weakest.The McLaren on the other hand has a more aesthetically pleasing placing and the fact that it all connects together also adds to the aesthetics. My sentiments are that as long as it achieves the objective, why go for ugly when it can be visually appealing to the eye?Red Bull on the other hand externally looks like it has made the fewest changes to compensate for the altitude in Mexico. Perhaps it was overcooled at other races but I would doubt this - as most teams will push the limits for each individual track.That's all the engine and its ancillary cooling requirement changes compared. The other big cooling requirement is for the brakes and it's difficult to see who has done the best job there.For the teams, it's difficult to simulate those early race laps when the car is at its heaviest and you are running in traffic; when the brakes overheat, the only way to cool them down is to use them less - which means more lifting and coasting.So, who has done the best job on all of this while minimising the aerodynamic losses? I think it's going to be Sunday night before we know that.

item.title: 'They’ve destroyed cycling' - Bardiani-CSF-7 Saber boss gives scathing assessment of the UCI after Italian team unable to race Giro d’Italia in 2027
item.author: Dan Challis
item.content:encoded: Veteran team boss Bruno Reverberi has called the UCI “incompetent” after his Bardiani-CSF-7 Saber team finished outside of the UCI’s top-30 rankings in 2026, making them ineligible to race a Grand Tour next season. Reverberi said that it is likely that Bardiani-CSF-7 Saber will shutter due to the current regulations, which he says are making teams at the ProTeam level increasingly fragile, with no guarantees of invitation to the world’s biggest races. The long-standing team has raced every edition of the Giro d’Italia since 1982 and is well known for its attacking style. Bardiani-CSF-7 Saber has been a fruitful breeding ground for Italian talent over the years, including the team’s last Giro stage-winner, Giulio Ciccone, who won in Sestola in 2016. Sonny Colbrelli and Giulio Pellizzari are two other names to have emerged through this system.The team has also been involved in several doping scandals over the years, with the likes of Emanuele Sella and Stefano Pirazzi banned during their time on the team.“Our project is to stop,” Reverberi told the “How can you spend €5 million and not have the right to race? There is no future, and cycling has no future. We have already thought about closing in two years. In fact, we have taken four or five new riders and made them sign for only one year.”“You don’t even have the courage to go to the sponsor and ask for money,” he said, despite signing a “multi-year agreement” with Uzbek clothing company 7 Saber at the start of this season.Reverberi’s main charge towards the UCI is its points system, which he believes is encouraging teams to race for top-10s rather than chase glory in the breakaway.It is perhaps the team’s reticence to play the game as other teams have done which left them languishing down the UCI points rankings, 121 below Euskaltel-Euskadi, who travelled to Algeria and Panama in the last weeks of the 2026 season in their search for points.“Our way of racing was to break away,” he said. “Now you don’t even break away, because you try to keep the rider there to sprint for tenth place for those damned UCI points,” he said.“The UCI is incompetent. They’ve destroyed cycling,” he concluded, suggesting that while the top of the sport explodes in its popularity and financial investment, the lower-level is breaking apart.“We’ve reached a bit of a peak with Pogačar in some ways, but everything is falling apart underneath,” he said. “Cycling is disappearing, and nobody’s looking at it.”The road season might be at an end, but Cyclingnews isn't slowing down. item.title: Knicks Bulletin: ‘Josh said he feels the fatigue?’
item.author: Antonio Losada
item.content:encoded: The Sixers beat the Knicks on Friday……meaning they are 2-0 in the head-to-head matchup. That’s it, that’s all it means. No parade down Broad Street.Here’s what we heard coming out of Cheesesteak Arena.On losing to the 76ers in the NBA Cup:“I don’t look it as a statement game. It’s the next game in front of us. Obviously, it’s a [NBA] Cup game and you always want to push yourself to have an opportunity to try and win something. This means taking a step toward that goal.“But I just want to get a little better every time we play. These guys really hurt us in transition last game. Our transition defense right now stinks. But it’s gotten a little better. Tonight, it will be tested. Obviously Jaylen is not playing and he’s one of the best in transition. You look at little things and you hope to get better at the little things while getting a win.”On the Knicks allowing Philadelphia to attack the paint too easily:“They were getting in our paint left and right, right and left, and it was really, really easy doing it.”On the Knicks forcing difficult plays instead of executing simple offense:“It’s been going on all year. Like, we’re trying to hit a home run every time we get the ball. And we have to hit singles. We can’t hit a home run. We gotta hit singles offensively and then if our play breaks down, we have to move. There’s too many times where we have too many guys trying to iso and the other four guys sitting there and staring at the ball a whole possession.”On the Knicks improving their turnover management in the second half:“We did a better job with our turnovers (in the second half). But more importantly, we reacted better when we turned the ball over and we had five turnovers for six points (against).”On the Knicks failing to maintain their focus throughout an entire game:“Against a good team on the road, if you let go of those things in a half, you’re in trouble. And so somehow some way we have to be cognizant of doing this stuff for 48 minutes, which we’re not doing right now.“Tonight it was the first half and it was almost like [we thought] we’re just gonna show up and go hoop and not do the little things that we need to do to go get a win.”On the importance of executing the fundamentals consistently:“It’s a little thing here, a little thing there, a little thing there. … We’re competitive when we need to be and that’s why all of our games that we’re in we have a chance down the stretch, but trying to make sure we continue to do the little things throughout the course of the game is gonna be huge for us because we’re not doing it right now.”On LeBron James making decisive plays against the Knicks:“[LeBron’s] a great player, and when you have a great player out there, with his ability, he’s gonna make plays, and he made big plays down the stretch. It’s the NBA, and it’s not surprising when a guy like Maxey or LeBron or Jalen makes a big play. You just hope that it doesn’t come down to that all the time.”On Ernie Johnson’s retirement announcement and his impact on NBA coverage:“I’d like to give a quick shoutout to Ernie Johnson. I don’t know him well. Obviously I know him from the TV. I try not to watch a lot of basketball shows because it gets me too high or gets me too low. But their show is one that I always get good laughs at.“Just from afar, Ernie seems like he’s a big time human being. And the little bit I know about his story, it’s fascinating. He will be sorely missed, not only from the fans out there and other media members, but I know from a coaching standpoint too in keeping everything light and enjoyable and all that other stuff.“So I hope you have a heck of a year, Ernie. We’re gonna all miss you, but thanks for doing what you do to make people smile everyday.”On the Knicks’ careless turnovers and hesitant decision-making:“Just a little careless. And sometimes it can be us being hesitant as well, wanting to make the right play, but they’re also not trying to turn over, and then it’s just a little late to our decision-making. It could be a lot of things, but obviously, we got to clean it up.”On Josh Hart’s fatigue excuse six games into the season:“Josh said he feels the fatigue? Well, Josh is old as s–t, so.”On the Knicks needing to learn from their losses and stop relying on comebacks:“I’ve said in the past that it’s always important to learn from wins. Obviously, you learn from losses, as well. There have been plenty of times that we’ve learned from being down. In those same games, we’ve made adjustments to where we weren’t down anymore and came back and won the game. Obviously, we have to understand what we need to do. It’s starting the game that way. I think that has to be our biggest point of emphasis going forward.“I thought we played decent in the second half, took care of the ball better, played better defense, but we have to put a full 48 minutes together.”On the Knicks lacking energy against Philadelphia:“Today we played like a team that was on the end of a road trip. We gotta find that gear. We gotta find that energy.“We picked up the pace in the second half, but what makes this team special is doing it for 48 minutes. We didn’t do that tonight. We put ourselves in a bad spot, and give credit to the team over there. They hit the shots when they needed to. We just got to execute at a higher level.”On escaping the Knicks’ offensive struggles too late against the 76ers:“I thought we did a great job in that fourth quarter of finding that gear, like you said, just kind of getting out of the quicksand. To do that puts us in a position where you gotta make some magic happen, and we just didn’t have enough magic tonight.”On the challenge of facing LeBron James and the 76ers:“They’re a great team. Obviously, you have arguably the greatest player of all time. We’ve got to bring our best. We’ve got to execute at a high level. And we’ve got to continue to use these games as a learning experience.”On the Knicks’ stagnant offense and lack of movement:“It’s a new year. I think we’re trying to work our way into the season. But I think the flow’s tougher. Sometimes the ball is stagnant, I think that’s a little bit from fatigue and not a mental thing. You know what the other team is doing, and physically you’re trying to get your body to get to that point. So I think that that’s part of it. We got to be more deliberate with cuts and movements. And taking care of the ball.”On the Knicks feeling fatigued after playing three games in four nights:“We all feel the fatigue. So we got to fight through it. Six games in. So we got to find a way to make sure we get our bodies ready to play every day. I think mentally we’re there. We just gotta find it physically.”On the Knicks needing to execute more consistently:“We gotta find a way to execute better. And do that continuously.”On why the Knicks keep falling behind by double digits before attempting comebacks:“I wish I could tell you that one. If I could tell you that one, and the reason why, then maybe it would stop happening. I think we all have a great will to win. I think sometimes it takes us a little longer to find a game, whether that’s the flow, fatigue, whatever it is.“We have to do a better job of finding the game early, making it easy and then not relying on double-digit comebacks because it’s taxing.”On LeBron James’ performance against the Knicks:“He’s been good, but tonight, I thought that was his best game for sure. I thought he was good all the way through tonight. I thought he got some downhill stuff. He used his size and knocked them around a little bit for some layups. I thought he obviously pushed the ball and got us organized. I thought he was a little quicker to make some decisions to shoot the 3-ball as well. And then, he obviously made those couple of big plays down the stretch.”On how New York’s off-court opportunities can distract players after winning a championship:“When you win a championship, especially in New York, you have all these different opportunities off the court that take place. You’re filming commercials, you’re having these different shows, you’re doing these different things. All these events are happening.“You’ve got to try to narrow it back down and lock in on basketball because playing in New York, you can get a little bit taken away from the sport with all the activities that go along with being in New York City. But you have to now try to narrow it down back to basketball. Key in, lock in on basketball. Make it the main priority and build out from there.”On why the Knicks deserved to celebrate their championship throughout the offseason:“That’s normal. That’s a part of human nature, man. You win a championship for the New York Knicks. You kidding me? After 53 years, you gotta enjoy that. You will never be the first one to win it after 53 years ever again.“So that energy, you have to capitalize on it. It’s just a matter of now being able to kind of channel that and now focus on basketball and lock in a little bit more.”On whether the Knicks’ slow start is concerning:“I’m not concerned. When you are the champions, man, every target is at your back. Every team’s gunning for you, so it’s tough to kind of get off to a great start the following year. I’m not concerned. I think it’s a matter of just kind of locking in and focusing a little bit more, and they’ll be okay.”

item.title: 'It really feels like a victory' - Belgian cyclo-cross champion returns to training following surgery for cardiac arrhythmias
item.author: Dan Challis
item.content:encoded: Two-time Belgian national champion Marion Norbert Riberolle has restarted training after the opening to her 2026/2027 cyclo-cross campaign was halted due to a cardiac arrhythmia.The Crelan-Corendon rider opened her season in Dendermonde and also raced the Kermiscross on the 15th of October before undergoing surgery to address the issue that was causing her heart to beat with an irregular rhythm. After several sessions on the indoor trainer, Norbert Riberolle has now resumed training outdoors. She is being closely monitored by her team’s medical staff, and a decision is yet to be made regarding her return to racing.“After several successful sessions on the rollers, she has now also taken to the road for the first time again. Our staff is monitoring everything closely so that it can be determined later when our Belgian champion can make a restart.”In Norbert Riberolle’s absence, Lucinda Brand (Baloise Verzekeringen-Het Poetsbureau Lions) has been dominating on the 'cross field, already taking three victories this season.Born in France and originally racing under a French license, Norbert Riberolle switched allegiances in 2021. She won the under-23 cyclo-cross world championships in 2020 and claimed three victories last season, including her second Belgian national title. The rider born in Troyes also races on the road for Fenix-Premier Tech’s development team. “I am doing very well and I feel that I have recovered well. The rest has done me good,” she said.“The first training sessions on the rollers went without problems, and in the meantime, I have also completed my first ride outdoors. It really feels like a victory. I was incredibly happy to be back on the bike and to be able to train outside.”The road season might be at an end, but Cyclingnews isn't slowing down. item.title: Yankees Birthday of the Day: Matt Nokes
item.author: Jonathan Farrar
item.content:encoded: Growing up in the Southern California sunshine, Matt Nokes had the kind of baseball profile most travel-ball dads dream their sons will have: a lefty-hitting catcher. That combination eventually helped him reach the majors. Nokes’ path to the pros started when the Giants drafted him in the 20th round of the 1981 MLB Draft out of Patrick Henry High School in San Diego. A decade later, it took him to New York.October 31, 1963 (San Diego, CA) 1990-94After being drafted, Nokes started working his way toward the show, beginning in Rookie ball while still just 17 years old. He spent the next two seasons playing in Single-A, though his first year at the level was a bit of a struggle. In his second season, Nokes broke out with Fresno, slashing .322/.410/.508 with 14 home runs. The performance was good enough to earn him a promotion.Nokes spent the 1984 season in Double-A and returned to the level to start the 1985 season. After another solid year, the Giants gave him a September call-up. In 19 games for San Francisco, he hit .208 and launched his first two major-league home runs. The Giants used Nokes as part of a package that offseason, sending him and pitchers Eric King and Dave LaPoint to Detroit in exchange for Bob Melvin, Juan Berenguer, and a player to be named later (Scott Medvin).Now in the Tigers organization, Nokes returned to Double-A to start the 1986 season. Detroit gave him another cup of coffee at the end of the year before moving on from longtime starting catcher Lance Parrish that offseason, opening the door for Nokes to take over behind the plate.Nokes’ rookie year was by far the best season of his career. In 1987, he slashed .289/.345/.536 with 32 home runs and 87 RBIs. He was selected to the All-Star team and won the Silver Slugger Award, but finished third in Rookie of the Year voting behind Mark McGwire and Kevin Seitzer. It was quite a debut for the young catcher, who helped Detroit win the AL East — the Tigers’ last playoff appearance for nearly two decades.After that amazing season, Nokes came back down to earth and saw his playing time and production slip over the next two and a half seasons in Detroit. The Tigers decided it was time to move on in 1990 and traded him to the Yankees that summer for the elder Lance McCullers and Clay Parker.The Yankees hoped Nokes’ bat could help the struggling club, particularly against right-handed pitching. With Bob Geren and Rick Cerone also on the roster, Nokes split time behind the plate and at designated hitter. He batted .238 with eight home runs in 92 games for New York. After the season, Cerone departed, and Nokes entered 1991 as the Yankees’ primary backstop.In his first full season in pinstripes, Nokes played 135 games. In 493 at-bats, he hit .268 with 24 home runs. Those 24 round-trippers led the team, while his 77 RBIs were good for second. Those Yankees were lousy, but it was hardly his fault.The 1992 season saw Nokes top 20 home runs for the second straight year, finishing with 22. His average dropped to .224, and his on-base percentage fell to .293. Mike Stanley also began pushing for more playing time behind the plate.Shifted into more of a reserve role, Nokes appeared in 56 games as a catcher and another 11 at designated hitter in 1993. He slashed .249/.303/.424 with 10 home runs. The highlight of his Yankees tenure came on September 4th, when he was behind the plate for Jim Abbott’s no-hitter against the Cleveland.Heading into the 1994 season, Nokes was still slotted behind Stanley on the depth chart. However, a broken bone in his hand in April sidelined him for much of the season. With the players’ strike ending the season in August, Nokes was limited to just 28 games. He batted .291 with seven home runs in his final season in pinstripes. The Yankees’ last game of the season came on August 11th, bringing Nokes’ time in the Bronx to an abrupt end.Nokes spent the 1995 season with the Orioles and Rockies, appearing in 36 games between the two clubs. That ended up being his final major league season, though he continued playing in independent leagues later in his career. He also spent time coaching and eventually returned to the San Diego area, where he has worked as a hitting instructor and consultant, doing what he can to give back to the game.Happy Halloween to all, and happy birthday, Matt!See more of the “Yankees Birthday of the Day” series here.

item.title: 'I still need some time to analyse what I really want' - Tadej Pogačar to return to the UAE Tour, but 2027 race calendar still undecided with Tour de France the main target
item.author: Dan Challis
item.content:encoded: Tadej Pogačar has already confirmed his main ambitions for the 2027 race season; a sixth Tour de France title, a fourth world title and a shot at redemption at the Vuelta a España. In the coming weeks, alongside the management team at UAE Team Emirates-XRG, his race calendar leading up to those objectives will be finalised. According to the Slovenian, on the cards is a return to the UAE Tour, a race he won in 2021, 2024 and 2025. He skipped the race of his team’s homeland in 2026 and began his season at Strade Bianche. Speaking on a virtual community ride on MyWhoosh, the UAE-owned training platform which sponsors his team, Pogačar said that there was a “big chance” that he will then return to the Spring Classics, with that elusive victory at Paris-Roubaix surely a focus. His comments will come as a blow to the organisers of the Tour Down Under, who have said that they are “doing everything we can” to bring Pogačar to Adelaide in January. This option appeared more likely due to Pogačar’s early season ending after his crash at the Vuelta a España. It is also one of just a handful of WorldTour stage races that Pogačar is yet to win.The 28-year-old raced five one-day races and the Tours de Romandie and Suisse ahead of claiming his record-equalling fifth Tour de France title in 2026. Pogačar then competed in the Vuelta a España for the second time in his career, crashing out on stage 8 while in the leader’s jersey and concluding his season.A final judgement on Pogačar’s race schedule will be made during a team training camp in December. "There's like three options that I can do. The team gave me three options of my calendar, but it's a big decision," he said during the community ride."I think I still need some time to really analyse what I really want for next year. And I think the final decision will be done in December, where we have another training camp."There's a big chance I come back to Classics for sure, and also UAE Tour, and obviously Tour de France. There's no hiding in this, I think, so we will see."Speaking to at a charity golf event two weeks ago, Pogačar stated his central ambitions for the season. "The goal for next year would obviously be the World Championships, combined with the Tour and the Vuelta. Even though I'd rather ride the Giro, I'll have to tick off the Vuelta at some point too. I think that will be the goal for next year," he said.While his season will once again orbit around success at the Tour de France, Pogačar admitted that he had not yet looked at the route for the 2027 race, which was presented on the 22nd of October."I didn't check a lot the route yet of the Tour. I was not there for the announcement,” he said. "Obviously the Tour is always three weeks long, and there's always big mountains, flat stages, tricky stages, some crosswinds, time-trials. So you always have everything.”"No matter which cities host the start or finish, it's always more or less the same and the toughest race in the world. You need to be ready for everything."The road season might be at an end, but Cyclingnews isn't slowing down. item.title: Why F1's 2026 cars are unusually quick in Mexico
item.author: Josh Suttill
item.content:encoded: A combination of factors means Formula 1's 2026 cars have been unusually close to the performance of their ground-effect predecessors in Mexico.Charles Leclerc's FP1-topping time, a 1m18.128s, was 0.252s quicker than the lap he set to lead first practice in Mexico last year. That's the first time the 2026 cars have outpaced the 2025 cars in an FP1 session, having usually been two or three seconds slower.Leclerc lowered the bar by three tenths to a 1m17.827s in FP2, though that was 0.435s slower than Max Verstappen's FP2 benchmark from last year.Pirelli's pre-weekend simulations had predicted a 1m17.0s would be pole position, but after Friday's running it's now predicted to be well below that.Pole position last year - a 1m15.586s - ended up being 1.8s faster than the pace in FP2, so you'd expect the 2026 pole position to be in the low-1m16s.That should mean the smallest 2025 versus 2026 dry-weather qualifying difference of the season, with the previous closest being 1.409s in Baku.So why are the 2026 cars so competitive at the Mexican Grand Prix relative to their ground-effect-era predecessors?A resurfaced, busier trackThe track underwent a partial resurfacing ahead of the 2026 race, with resurfacing work taking place from Turn 10 to Turn 1."This could also be an effect," Pirelli's chief engineer Simone Berra said."Obviously it was partially resurfaced, so sector one and half of sector two didn't have this kind of new Tarmac, so that could be a contribution also, but it's not the only explanation about why we were so fast, or faster than we expected."Another explanation Pirelli offered is the track being in better condition because there's more support series laying down rubber this year.However, there has only been a 10-minute increase in the on-track action prior to FP1 versus last year, with the one-make GTM Super Copa series, Masters Historic and Formula 4 NACAM championship on the support bill this year."I think part of these results are due to the track in better conditions compared to last year, we have several supporting series that are helping," Berra said."All the supporting series run before FP1 and between FP1 and FP2, so the track was evolving quite a lot during the day."Less of a penalty at altitudeThe most important factor is Mexico's high altitude is also less detrimental to the performance of the 2026 cars and power units than the 2025 packages. There's less total downforce to lose in the first place and the ground-effect cars were more downforce-dependent."The conditions, the altitude here, it's in favour of these cars compared to the old one," Berra said."The old cars were losing more downforce, compared to what this car generation are losing."Also, the other point is that the engine can push more compared to a normal situation or sea level conditions."So that's the main point, the drivers can push and so the difference with laptimes from last year are reduced."Altitude, of course, does not effect the electrical power, which is far more influential on performance with the 2026 power units.The 2026 cars (Leclerc's lap in red) are quicker on the straights than the 2025 cars (Verstappen's lap in blue), with the 2026 machines over four tenths up on the run to the Turn 4 left-hander. And it should be noted that Leclerc's Ferrari is one of the weakest in this section among the top-four teams because of its power unit deficit. So the gap is even larger if you compare to Verstappen's 2026 car.The 2026 cars quickly lose that built-up advantage in the low-speed corners that follow and never recover it, but the drop-off is far less stark than at other circuits such as Spa (3.799s between 2025 and 2026 poles) and Monza (2.994s between them).The cars actually end up relatively energy-rich in Mexico, so it's one of the better tracks for showcasing the performance of these cars.

item.title: Seabirds racing home over the ocean can get jet-lagged
item.author: John Timmer
item.content:encoded: Flying across several time zones often causes jet lag, a feeling when the body insists it's the middle of the night while the clock says it's lunchtime. Now it turns out this nuisance is not exclusive to humans.A new Science study on Manx shearwaters, seabirds that can fly hundreds of kilometers a day over the North Atlantic, shows they jet-lag themselves during their excursions. And because these birds navigate by the Sun, that jet lag leaves a measurable mark—it skews their compass.Patrick Lewin is a behavioral and sensory ecologist at the University of Oxford and lead author of the study. “Manx shearwaters are medium-sized birds, about the same size as a pigeon,” Lewin said. “They are white underneath and black on top, but they have very long wings, and they are closely related to albatross.” Manx shearwaters nest in burrows on coastal islands around the North Atlantic. Most breed around the UK and Ireland, with about half of their population living in Wales.

item.title: 'I think things could have been done better' - Visma-Lease a Bike departee regrets slow development on Dutch team as he drops to continental level for 2027
item.author: Dan Challis
item.content:encoded: 24-year-old Loe van Belle is leaving the Dutch squad after three seasons, plus two in its development team. Once viewed as a promising Classics rider and time-triallist, Van Belle was informed in the summer that his services were no longer required.Speaking in an interview with Van Belle has lamented his development while on the team, suggesting that things could have been done better, both by himself and the backroom staff. Crashes, injuries and an iliac artery flow limitation also played roles in his inability to prove his potential, ultimately leading to his departure. “I look back on my years at Visma-Lease a Bike with a good feeling,” he told “When you look at the guidance and what you learn there as a rider in terms of tactics, racing style, and preparation for races and training camps, I don’t think you could have a better training ground. I benefited enormously from that, and I appreciate that immensely.“But when I look at my physical development, I think things could have been done better, both from the team and from myself.”Van Belle’s ability was clear as an under-23 rider, when he won a stage at the Flanders Tomorrow Tour and finished 9th at the 2022 Tour de l’Avenir. He was promoted to the WorldTour team in 2024 and was utilised as a domestique for the most part, picking up a handful of top-10 results during his three seasons on the team. While Van Belle is appreciative of the investment that Visma-Lease a Bike gave to him, he now believes that he should have spoken up for himself when it was clear that he wasn’t progressing as planned.“I want to look at myself first and foremost. I should have been more professional in taking responsibility for my own career.“I have actually always very politely complied with what others said. That is how I was raised, too. If someone tells you what to do, especially when it is your boss, you do it. You assume that it is best for you. But over the past two years, I have regularly asked myself what I missed out on.“Shouldn't I have taken more responsibility to get the most out of my career? Shouldn't I have chosen myself a little more now and then, or banged my fist on the table more? Perhaps my situation would look different now. Do I blame myself for that? I think so, actually,” he said.Van Belle never raced a Grand Tour with the team and has signed for Dutch continental outfit BEAT CC p/b Saxo for the 2027 season. His hope now is to return to the professional ranks in the future, having overcome health issues that have limited him.Along with a concussion after a crash at GP de Denain this year, which kept him away from racing for six weeks, the native of Zoetermeer had an iliac artery operation in 2025 - a procedure to ease a lack of blood flow, which is common for cyclists. “I had probably been riding around with that for three and a half years. After that surgery, it felt like a mental brake was released. Finally, I could race freely again, without constantly being afraid that I wouldn't be able to continue after just one effort,” he said of his iliac artery issue.“That blockage was huge, not only physically but also mentally. Together with the team, we tried to figure out what was going on. But precisely during that period, in hindsight, I perhaps should have taken more responsibility myself. I will take that lesson with me.”After the surgery, Van Belle made progress on the bike and hoped for a renewed contract for 2027. However, Visma-Lease a Bike decided to let the rider go, bringing in British rider Mark Donovan from Pinarello-Q36.5 and Belgian Matisse van Kerckhove from the development team.The road season might be at an end, but Cyclingnews isn't slowing down.
