item.title: The academy system needs a refresh but now is the time for Carrick to trust in youth | David Pleat
item.author: David Pleat
item.content:encoded: Manchester United’s most famous eras were built around their academy products, so why not give the current crop a chance to shine?Watching Manchester United succumb meekly against Comoand Bournemouth brought to mind questions and comparisons with yesteryear. Two of United’s most famous eras were built around their youth players: the Busby Babes and the Class of ’92. Could this be a moment for Michael Carrick to give their most talented academy products a meaningful chance?In February 2025 I saw United beat Arsenal 3-2 in the FA Youth Cup at the Emirates Stadium. Jack and Tyler Fletcher did well for United and so did Harry Amass, a signing from Watford. Max Dowman, a generational talent, starred for Arsenal.Continue reading...

item.title: 2027 Nissan Rogue Hybrid: Drives like an EV, but there's no plug involved
item.author: Jonathan M. Gitlin
item.content:encoded: Nissan has a new version of its bestselling Rogue SUV, and it’s launching the model here with the latest version of its e-Power hybrid system, which Ars tested in February. Most hybrid cars you can buy today are parallel hybrids, which means that they have an internal combustion engine and an electric motor, both of which drive some or all of the wheels—everything works in parallel. But there’s another approach. Instead of connecting the engine to the wheels via a transmission, it can act as a generator and charge the traction battery, which in turn powers the electric motor. Since the engine and motor work in series, this is known as a series hybrid.That’s mostly how the Chevrolet Volt worked. As does Honda’s hybrid CR-V. Well, mostly; engineers worked out it was more efficient for those cars' gasoline engines to directly drive the wheels at highway speeds, something that to this day makes a certain subset of hybrid car enthusiasts irrationally angry. If you know anyone like that in your life, send them to wherever the nearest Nissan dealership is, because the 2027 Rogue Hybrid is exactly what they’ve been asking for.Under the hood, with its crisp shut line and slim horizontal lights that give me something of a Range Rover vibe, there’s a 1.5 L, three-cylinder turbocharged direct-injection engine that generates 148 hp (110 kW). It only revs to 5,200 rpm because it’s optimized to charge the battery, not cope with the various loads of an engine connected to a gearbox and the wheels. That also allows the engine to operate at a rather impressive 42 percent thermal efficiency—we would need to look at Formula 1 engines to find higher.

item.title: Review: You Can See Everything blurs the view of Elizabeth Holmes' deceit
item.author: Jennifer Ouellette
item.content:encoded: In 2015, biomedical entrepreneur Elizabeth Holmes was Silicon Valley's golden girl, lauded as the youngest and richest self-made female billionaire thanks to the company she founded, Theranos, which was valued at $9 billion at the height of its success. Then it all came crashing down when accusations of fraud surfaced about the company's signature blood-testing device, culminating in a sensational trial. Holmes was convicted on four counts and sentenced to 11 years in prison.Holmes is back in the headlines thanks to a new film, , which depicts the final days before Holmes, having exhausted her appeals, went to prison. Co-directed by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, it's a surreal, absurdist piece that has largely been received with gushing enthusiasm and no small amount of hype, with some declaring it the best film of the year. A few contrarian voices have emerged over the past week with much-needed reality checks, but there's no denying the film is destined to be an awards-season darling.Pardon me for joining the buzzkills, but I cannot in good conscience jump on the bandwagon. Sure, it has its moments, and the second half is highly entertaining, but there's nothing here to warrant all the breathless hyperbole. For all their much-touted access, Oppenheim and Fielder have produced a surprisingly shallow film that runs in circles, yielding very little fresh or novel insight—into Holmes, personally, or much else.

item.title: Wind tunnel tested: The UCI-illegal Merida Reacto One was designed to beat the wind tunnel tests – it failed, but that's only half the story
item.author: josh.croxton@futurenet.com (Josh Croxton)
item.content:encoded: By every objective measure, the Reacto One isn't a groundbreaking bike, but subjectively it's brilliant. A really enjoyable bike to ride, and I love that Merida went a bit wild. Progressive spec.Comfortable ride with confident handling.Value for money is pretty good, when compared to others of this level.Sub-par aero performance despite having an unfair advantage.Heavier than competitor bikes of similar aero performance.UCI-illegal bars could cause issues if you want to race it.72%The Merida Reacto One is a bike that confuses me. It sort of proves you can't always judge a book by its cover. But then again, it sort of proves you can. With its narrow handlebars, one-by (Classified-equipped) groupset, deep wheels and aero tubes, it looks as if it was designed to 'win' the wind tunnel tests performed by ourselves and other media.It should have been a prime candidate for the top spot in our aero bike wind tunnel testing, but it fell remarkably short of the current leaders, Factor's One and Cervélo's S5, landing a disappointing result; the details of which are below. It was better than the older Reacto we tested in 2025, but despite being a full-house bingo card of go-faster tricks that make it UCI-illegal and are undoubtedly an unfair advantage compared to other bikes, it barely scraped the top 10. But then when I climbed aboard it and rode it in earnest, I liked almost everything about it. The position was great, the handling was superb, it was plenty responsive under power, and it was decently comfortable. £9,500.00 / $N/A / €11,000.007.73kg (no pedals, computer or bottles).3XS, 2XS, XS, S, M, L, XL Shimano Dura-Ace x Classified Powershift, Rotor Aldhu crank DT Swiss Arc 1100 65mmRed/Silver, Silver/Black 32mm (with room to spare)52T chainset x 11-30 cassette as tested, plus Classified PowershiftThe Merida Reacto One is the black sheep in the wider Reacto range. All of the other Reacto Models are 'normal' in that they come with two-by groupsets from Shimano or SRAM, and handlebars that are UCI-legal in their width. The One – not to be confused with the Factor One (or even the Trek Mad(One)) – is a showcase of what the product team can create when they're let a little loose. The Taiwanese brand partnered with some revered European brands to kit the bike out with the set menu from the aero playbook. DT Swiss supplied its ARC 1100 Dicut 65mm deep wheels, Continental supplied the Aero 111 front tyre, and Classified chipped in its Powershift rear-hub gear system, which in turn meant Rotor could supply a 1x aero chainring alongside its InSpider power meter chainset. Perhaps most pertinent of all, though, is that Vision supplied a super-narrow, special edition Merida Team CW 1P cockpit that measured a grand total of just 22.5cm between the Shimano Dura-Ace hoods. And no, I've not got the hoods set up tilted inwards like a 2022 WorldTour pro.It's an off-the-shelf version of what I think I'd build for the type of crit racing that suits me best – flat, fast and tightly packed, rather than hilly or too punchy. Deep wheels, one-by groupset, big chainring, small cassette, narrow bars and aero frame. The Classified groupset is a nice touch, and one that means you get the aerodynamics of one-by without compromising on gear range or steps, meaning you can actually live with it and ride it at the weekend without messing about with swapping wheels or cassettes around. I like it. It's well thought out.Notably, and this perhaps goes some way to explain why it didn't storm to victory in our wind tunnel test, that narrow cockpit is mainly achieved through a massive flare from the tops to the drops, as the outside-to-outside measurement down there is actually 42cm.When we test in the wind tunnel, we do so with our hands in the drops, meaning the narrow bars didn't really have an opportunity to shine. If I'd performed the same test in more of an aero position with hands on the hoods, horizontal forearms and elbows bent to 90°, the narrowness would have probably made a difference. It would have also been less comparable to other bikes and thus, less of a fair test. Also, I can't hold that position for more than a few minutes at a time, and I'm going to bet that not many others can either. On the flip side, it only takes a few minutes at a time to make the difference in a race sometimes, so you can spin it that way if you prefer.Elsewhere, the bike promises 32mm tyre clearance front and rear. The 29mm Aero 111 tyre up front measured at exactly 29mm on the DT Swiss wheels, and the clearance measured amply at 12mm either side, so you could easily go wider if you wanted. At the rear, the 30mm GP5000 S TR tyre measured at 31mm, with 6mm of room to spare on either side according to our calipers, so you could probably get away with a little more than claimed, but not much. Perhaps 34mm if you're in need of cobble-smoothing comfort.And while I'm on the subject of measuring, the Reacto One tipped our scales at a not-bad-but-not-excellent 7.73kg (weighed without pedals, computer mount, or bottle cages). Okay, I've dallied long enough. Time to get stuck into the stuff you're really here for. As with all our wind tunnel tests, we took the Reacto to the Silverstone Sports Engineering Hub, tested it back-to-back against our baseline bike (as well as a handful of other competitors on the same day), to measure how aerodynamic it is. Using its comparison against that baseline bike, which remains unchanged between tests, we can also measure it against bikes we've tested in years gone by.We test every bike in three separate setups: the bike on its own first, then the bike with a rider, then finally we swap in a 'control' wheelset to isolate the differences found in the frame/fork and cockpit. We test each of these setups across seven distinct wind angles – -15°, -10°, -5°, 0°, 5°, 10°, and 15° – for a total of 21 different measurements. And we test at a wind speed of 40km/h, for either 15 or 30 seconds per measurement, depending on whether it's with or without a rider. Everything that can be controlled remains unchanged between tests, including the tyres, the bottles, the clothing and so on, and we do our best to ensure the bike setup and rider position are the same across all tests, no matter what bike is being tested. Starting with the raw measurements for the two tests without a rider. This doesn't tell us too much, aside from that the DT Swiss Wheels tested slightly faster than our Enve SES 4.5 control wheels, especially at higher yaw angles. Hardly a surprise given the depth difference. From here, as we do with all our tests, I've run some calculations and applied weightings to land on an average that's relevant to real world conditions. From here, we can then see how many watts the Reacto One saves against our baseline. As suggested at the top of this review, I'm pretty disappointed to see it down in 11th place. Don't get me wrong, that's still a reasonable result and one that puts aero bikes like the Giant Propel, Canyon Aeroad and X-Lab AD9 to shame, not to mention its own predecessor, but I was expecting more for a bike that pulled out all the aero tricks.The Reacto One is exactly four watts behind the Factor One, and very much on par with the new Enve Melee v2, which is much more of an all-rounder in its design. Next up, things don't really get any better when we swap in our control wheels…We only introduced the control wheel test in 2025, so some of the older bikes are missing, but the Reacto is still mid-table, approximately five watts behind the Factor One. The Cannondale SuperSix even climbs ahead, which is another all-rounder. We're splitting hairs, of course; it's still 35 watts better than our baseline bike, but I can't help but feel disappointed with its result. Next up, let's check what happens when we chuck a rider on the bike. At first glance, things start to look a little rosier here. At certain wind angles, the Merida is actually faster than the Factor One, which remains our benchmark (even though the Cervelo S5 snuck ahead by a fraction once the weightings had been applied). But this only really happens at the wider yaw angles, which we know aren't seen anywhere near as commonly in the real world. Therefore, when we get to the averaged result, the rankings are as follows. The big caveat to this data is that our error margin is bigger than many of the differences between the bikes, so the Reacto lay claim to a victory, but it be right near the bottom of the table. But taking the results as they come, the Reacto One is once again around five watts behind the leaders, in 10th place. When it first arrived at HQ, I was reluctant to test the Reacto in our wind tunnel test at all. Clearly it's a bike designed to be aero, and part of me feared it would win the test and I'd forever have to caveat that "of course it won, it was specced with 22cm handlebars." But when it came to measuring up, the bar width at the drops was no narrower than our baseline bike. 42cm outside-to-outside. The 1x groupset is still a bit sneaky, but Merida does sell the bike like this, so why should I leave it off the test? Factor was radical and progressive when designing the ONE, and we tested that. Merida kept things relatively sane when designing the Reacto frame, but then applied that progressive mindset to the spec. Two routes to a similar end goal, really. If the Reacto One stormed to victory, I would be caveating this write-up heavily, saying you could also just fit a 1x groupset or narrow bars to any other bike, so the test was unfair and so on. And, well, you can, and that's pretty damning for Merida. Despite having a significant spec advantage, the Reacto still didn't challenge the top spots. But – and this is a very large but – I don't care. As it happens, I went from reviewing the Factor One straight onto the Merida, and while I appreciate I'm probably a bit boring for saying this, I'd take the Merida almost every time. Objectively, by a true performance yardstick, the Factor does most things better, particularly power transfer, sprinting, aerodynamics, steering directness, and holding pace when tanking along flat ground. But, subjectively, I still preferred riding the Reacto. I had a much nicer time on it every time I rode it, and whatever performance I was probably giving away didn't really feel worth stressing about.Power transfer felt plenty enough, albeit this is what stood out the most when comparing the two, mainly because it's so insanely good on the Factor. The narrow cockpit was easy to get used to, despite my inability to hold an aero-hoods position for more than a few minutes. The comfort through the bars made it a much better bike to ride, so I was more confident on descents, and I was able to ride for longer without feeling beat up. I couldn't go more than an hour without aches and pains on the Factor, but I did multiple four-hour rides on the Merida without issue. This isn't a head-to-head between just two bikes, but even compared to other bikes I've ridden lately, which includes the Tarmac SL9, the Merida is the one I've enjoyed most. It strikes a solid balance between being race-ready, something you can ride to the cafe at the weekend, and something you can do your intervals on after work in the evenings. It wasn't completely without fault, though. For one, I had a terrible time with the Aero 111 tyre up front, puncturing three times in a single ride and five times overall in my two months of testing. It's hard to say whether that's due to the narrowness of the DT Swiss wheels, the fragility of a TT tyre, or just a coincidental streak of bad luck. I also struggled to get on with the Classified Powershift drivetrain, which wasn't running as smoothly as I'd experienced before. The shift itself is instant, but there's still a small delay after you press the shift button. I found that sometimes it didn't register the click, and during that small delay, there's no feedback to confirm whether it's registered. So it was a case of click, wait, nothing, click again, shift! It's a first-world problem, but it was annoying no less. The one problem I can actually attribute to Merida, though, was that the plastic cap that sits over the steerer tube and cockpit bolts didn't fit properly. On one fateful trip over a cattle grid (aka Texas gates for those outside the UK), it came off and went on a little journey to the wrong side of the road, where it was duly run over by a passing car. I retrieved it, but you'll see how bent it is in the photos. And finally, to round off the negatives, the little metal grills that Merida insists on putting over its brake calipers are, to put it nicely, the devil. I have scars on my left ankle from repeatedly catching it. The best thing about them is that they're removable, and should be the first thing you do if you buy this bike. Sorry to the Merida designers reading this, but in your defence, it's a small thing to find so irksome, so the rest of the bike must be pretty good. At £9,500, for a bike with a progressive top-spec build, competitive (albeit not quite leading) aero performance, and a reasonable weight, I don't think you can complain too much, given the price of the aforementioned competitors. Here in the UK, it's £2,499 cheaper than a top-spec S-Works Tarmac SL9 - currently £11,999. Or £2,699 less than the Factor ONE (£12,199).It's still an inordinate amount of money to spend on a bike, but if you're in the market for a top-tier bike, it's a pretty good option as long as you're not going to want to upgrade your wheels anytime soon, as the Classified Powershift hub locks you into using the DT Swiss ones specced. It's not the cheapest in its class, though. For a comparison in the other direction, you can get a Canyon Aeroad CFR with Dura-Ace and very similar DT Swiss wheels (the same but 55mm instead of 65mm) for £1000 less. Having not ridden the latest Aeroad, I can't comment on a direct comparison, but it is a more 'normal' build with UCI-legal bars. Overall, I really liked the Reacto One. I like that a brand known for being safe, good value – dare I say boring? – has the wherewithal and panache to sell a bike with a UCI-illegal 22cm handlebar, rather than just selling it as a frameset and forcing people to make their own fun.And in execution, I think it has pulled it off. It's a bike that sits in a nice sweet spot between everyday liveable, race-day ready, and a little bit mad. Maybe, just maybe, I'm seeing a bike that's otherwise a little underwhelming through rose-tinted glasses because of its aero-ification and the factor that it brings. It's hard to say whether I'd have enjoyed riding the 10K or Pro models, with their more common specs, as much as I did this. But I think sometimes the objective comparison is allowed to give way to the subjective opinion. Aerodynamically, the results are okay. Top ten, not bad. Nothing to write home about, but the Merida Reacto One is a good bike. Testing scorecard and notesDeep wheels, aero tubes, 1x chainset, narrow bars. It looks fast standing still, and the paint scheme complements it7.7kg for a deep-everything aero bike isn't bad, but there are others with similar wind tunnel credentials that come out much lighter.A competitive result, but in the context of the spec, it's pretty underwhelming, and had it been specced 'normally' with 38cm bars and a 2x chainset, it probably would have languished in the bottom half.This is where it shines. Comfortable, confidence inspiring, fun, and well rounded. It didn't shine in any one area, but didn't feel like a let down either.£9.5k for a top-level, progressively specced bike is pretty good value, even if it's still a lot of money. It's not quite Canyon Aeroad CFR good, but it's impressive nonetheless.

item.title: Will Wout van Aert race cyclo-cross this winter? Even he's not sure yet
item.author: Matilda Price
item.content:encoded: Wout van Aert is continuing to be coy about his possible return to cyclo-cross this season, saying that his calendar is not yet decided but that he is "already getting the itch" to race in the mud.Whilst Van der Poel has not given all that much hope of him spending much time on the CX bike this winter, Van Aert has given his fans more reasons to be hopeful, particularly with the World Championships taking place in Belgium in January –It's the first time in six years that Worlds have been in his home country, and the first since 2016 that spectators will be allowed, with the 2021 Worlds taking place with no crowds due to the Covid pandemic."I'm already getting the itch," he admitted to . "But for me it is important to wait long enough and make a well-considered choice, because the road season follows immediately after the cyclo-cross season, for which I am ambitious."Having raced the Vuelta a España and Road World Championships, Van Aert has only recently switched focus to cyclo-cross, which is why he's hesitant to commit to a schedule just yet, despite the 'cross season being well underway."I've only been training for a week. The focus is still on the basics, and I haven’t done any specific work yet," he said. "Give me another three weeks to see what my fitness is like and how much more training I need before I'm race-ready. For now, nothing is set in stone."He confirmed that he will stay in Belgium until the start of December, and is then due on Visma-Lease a Bike road training camp on December 8.If that pattern of the last five years is to be repeated, Van Aert's debut – if he decides to race – is likely to come only towards the end of December, with a short but sweet campaign probably all that is possible before he must focus on road preparation, with his main goals at the Spring Classics coming only a few weeks after the conclusion of the 'cross calendar. Last year, he made his CX debut at the World Cup in Antwerp on December 20, and had intended to race through to at least mid-January, but his season was cut short when he injured his ankle at Exact Cross Mol on January 2.He could be tempted to lengthen his season this winter, though, with the World Championships taking place at home in Oostende at the end of January."A World Championship on home soil is more appealing than a World Championship that is far away," he said. "I already rode a World Championship in Oostende in 2021 without spectators, and I would love to get a taste of it with a large crowd."The road season might be at an end, but Cyclingnews isn't slowing down. item.title: Bahrain Victorious welcome third bike sponsor in three years as Factor returns to the men's WorldTour peloton
item.author: Owen Rogers
item.content:encoded: Bahrain Victorious are the latest team to announce a major equipment chance for 2027, swapping to Factor bikes after just one year on Bianchi machines.Factor has retained a place in the men’s peloton, with US ProTeam Modern Adventure riding the brand’s bikes – and the brand will step up as a title sponsor in 2027 – while Women's WorldTour team Human Powered Health have been riding Factor since 2024, a partnership which will continue into next season.The length of Bahrain’s deal with Factor is unspecified, with press releases from both the team and the brand stating "from 2027".Factor have been around for 10 years and recently launched their new Factor One, which is highly likely to be Bahrain’s bike of choice, though they will also have access to the brand’s climbing bike the Ostro VAM, with the One SP for time trials. And should they follow Modern Adventure's example from this year, they may even choose the Monza for Paris-Roubaix."We have found a fantastic partner in Factor, a brand that shares our performance ethos and our ambition to be the best," said Bahrain Victorious managing director Milan Eržen. "Factor is continuously innovating on the bike, with a huge focus on performance, which will enable our riders to have one of the best setups in the peloton."For us, it was important to find a partner that shares the same drive to continuously improve. We believe that by combining Factor’s engineering expertise with the knowledge and feedback of our riders and performance team, we can push the boundaries of performance together and give our riders every opportunity to win at the very highest level."Rob Gitelis, Factor's founder, also expressed his pleasure with the partnership, saying: "At Factor, we have always believed that racing at the pinnacle of the sport is fundamental to who we are. It’s where our ideas are challenged, where our engineering is tested, and where we continue to push ourselves forward. "Bahrain Victorious shares our ambition and our belief that performance comes from challenging what is possible. We see this partnership as much more than supplying bikes to a professional team. It’s an opportunity to work together, to innovate, and to compete against the very best. We are incredibly excited about what we can achieve together from 2027."Bahrain’s one-year partnership with Bianchi yielded only nine victories for the team, their fewest since the Covid affected 2020 season, so Matej Mohorič, Lenny Martinez and co. will be hoping for more success atop their Factor steeds.The road season might be at an end, but Cyclingnews isn't slowing down. item.title: Rocket Report: Winter is coming for Themis; Cowboy Space adds iron to the fire
item.author: Stephen Clark
item.content:encoded: Welcome to Edition 9.17 of the Rocket Report! It's been a while since an American company announced plans for a medium-lift new launch vehicle, but that's what happened this week when a startup named Cowboy Space revealed specs for its Big Iron rocket, named for the classic country-western song by Marty Robbins. I'm a huge fan of the name. Maybe Cowboy Space is striking while the iron is hot as the space industry frets over demand for launch outpacing supply. However, Cowboy Space lags far behind so many other launch providers nearing the launch pad with their medium-class rockets, and the company didn't have much hardware to show at this week's big reveal. In other words, don't mistake style for substance. But we're rocket fans at Ars, and we wish them luck.As always, we welcome reader submissions, and if you don't want to miss an issue, please subscribe using the box below (the form will not appear on AMP-enabled versions of the site). Each report will include information on small-, medium-, and heavy-lift rockets as well as a quick look ahead at the next three launches on the calendar.Virgin's new rocket plane reaches home port. The first of Virgin Galactic's new Delta-class rocket planes left its Arizona factory Wednesday for a trip to Spaceport America in neighboring New Mexico, where it will undergo preparations for a test campaign culminating in suborbital flights to the edge of space, Ars reports. Virgin Galactic expects the craft's first commercial spaceflight to take place "early" in the second quarter of 2027, but like every other projected date in aerospace, this should be taken with a grain of salt. Virgin Galactic halted commercial flights of its previous vehicle, VSS , in 2024.

item.title: 'In recent years, I put too much pressure on myself' – Failed search for a new team ends in retirement for former La Flèche Wallonne winner Dylan Teuns
item.author: James Moultrie
item.content:encoded: Former La Flèche Wallonne winner Dylan Teuns has announced his retirement after 12 years as a professional. At 34, the Belgian puncheur also won two stages of the Tour de France, a stage of the Critérium du Dauphiné, and GC titles at the Tour de Pologne, Tour de Wallonie, and the Arctic Race of Norway. After stints at BMC, Bahrain Victorious, Israel-Premier Tech, and most recently Cofidis, Teuns had confirmed before Il Lombardia that he was looking for a new team in 2027, not yet wanting his career to end. But on Thursday evening, Teuns confirmed that the search for a new squad was over and that he would be hanging up his wheels."What a ride it has been! It is time to say goodbye to the professional peloton," read a post from Teuns on Instagram. "I look back with immense pride and gratitude on a career in which I was able to fulfil my absolute childhood dreams."He explained the situation he found himself in during the summer to the Flemish press, having been without a confirmed contract before July for the first time in years. Despite meeting with three WorldTour teams in the subsequent months, Teuns was unable to find a place, and admitted that he didn't want to move to a smaller team just to extend his career."I had known for months that I was in a difficult situation. My spring didn't turn out the way I had hoped. As a result, I ended up in a contract situation I had never experienced before," he told . "The Tour had already started, and I hadn't signed anywhere yet. That caused extra stress. Almost every team repeated the same mantra: 'we need to rejuvenate'. Eventually, I held intensive talks with three WorldTeams and two ProTeams. The talks with those WorldTeams came to nothing. "When I was told by Lotto-Intermarché last Friday that they had no place for me, I consulted with Elke [His partner, ed.] and my parents. It was already clear in my mind at that point, but together with them, I weighed all the pros and cons once again. The conclusion was that I wouldn't be happier by choosing a smaller team."Teuns didn't want to reveal which two ProTeams he'd been in contact with, saying. "I would rather not reveal that. Out of respect. Because those teams are doing excellent work with limited resources, and I do not want to speak ill of them."But he was honest in stating how he still believed he was good enough to compete at the WorldTour level, despite his struggles to perform in recent years and match his stunning 2022 season form. "I really wanted to continue for another two years. With a team, WorldTour or WorldTour-worthy, that performs. Because I felt I still have the potential for it," he said. "The responsibility of leadership was no longer a must. I was perfectly happy to act as a lead-out man for a puncheur or contribute to the team in the top classics from a free role."The fact that I haven't been able to show that potential over the past two seasons gnaws at me. In recent years, I put too much pressure on myself. I had high expectations. But because the results failed to materialise, the pressure only increased. And even when I did have a good moment, I received little appreciation from the team involved."Having to accept his situation, Teuns could only look back on his best victories, singling out: a specific 20-day period from July 24 to August 13, 2027, when he took his maiden victory as a pro and eight in total as he burst onto the scene with BMC, his two Tour stage wins atop La Super Planche des Belles Filles and Le Grand-Bornand, and his triumph on the Mur de Huy ahead of Flèche Wallonne master Alejandro Valverde in 2022 as his career highlights. |I am proud of the versatility I was able to show: from a time trial victory in the Ruta del Sol to completing all five Monuments and all three Grand Tours," said Teuns. "To all the fans, teammates, and staff members who have backed me all these years along the road and in front of the screen: thank you! But a special thanks goes out to my parents, close friends, and girlfriend for having my back during the highs and the lows."Deep gratitude for my loyal, steady entourage over the years. Without you all, this dream would have never become reality. It is time for a new chapter, but the love for the bike remains forever. Merci!"The road season might be at an end, but Cyclingnews isn't slowing down. item.title: Paralympic champion cyclist Thomas Peyroton-Dartet provisionally suspended after positive EPO test
item.author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
item.content:encoded: The International Testing Agency (ITA) have announced that French cyclist Thomas Peyroton-Dartet has tested positive for Erythropoietin (EPO).41-year-old Peyroton-Dartet returned the adverse analytical finding on September 5 at the 2026 UCI Para-cycling Road World Championships in Huntsville, Alabama, USA, where he won gold in the C3 road race two days later."The ITA reports that a sample collected during an in-competition testing mission conducted by the ITA on 5 September 2026 during the 2026 UCI Para-cycling Road World Championships in Huntsville, Alabama, USA, from French rider Thomas Peyroton-Dartet has returned an AAF for EPO," the ITA announced on Friday, adding that Peyroton-Dartet has been provisionally suspended from racing as a result.EPO is a well-known substance in cycling, having come to prominence during the 1990s. EPO stimulates red blood cell production, increasing an athlete's oxygen-carrying capacity, and so is incredibly effective in endurance sports such as cycling. The EPO test was introduced at the 2000 Olympic Games in Sydney and was first carried out in road cycling at La Flèche Wallonne a year later."The rider has been informed of the case and has the right to request the analysis of the B-sample," continued the ITA statement."If the B-sample analysis is requested and confirms the result of the A-sample, the case will be considered as a confirmed anti-doping rule violation. If the B-sample analysis is not requested, the case will also go ahead as a confirmed anti-doping rule violation. The rider will have the opportunity to present his explanations for the result."Peyroton-Dartet's gold this year wasn't the first medal of his career. He won the C3 road race at the 2022 and 2023 UEC Para-Cycling European Championships and took road race silver at the 2025 Worlds. His biggest triumph, however, came in 2024 at his home Paralympic Games in Paris, where he scored gold in the C3 time trial and silver in the C1-3 road race.Peyroton-Dartet has been competing in para-cycling since 2021, when he hit a car while on a training ride. Since then, he has suffered from cerebellar ataxia, a neurological condition resulting in a loss of balance, poor coordination, and difficulties with speech and eye movements.As well as competing in para-cycling events, Peyroton-Dartet has raced on the road with the EuroCyclingTrips-CCN Continental team at races around the world, including the Chrono des Nations, Tour de Taiwan, Vuelta Asturias, Tour de Beauce, and Tour du Maroc.The road season might be at an end, but Cyclingnews isn't slowing down. item.title: Is virtual racing 'real' racing? – Our team weighs in on whether esports is 'legit' or 'just a fitness contest'
item.author: cyclingnews@cyclingnews.com (Cyclingnews)
item.content:encoded: Back in the day, the prospect of an indoor turbo trainer session (that's what we called them before they got smart, kids) would generally unite cyclists, who pretty much unanimously agreed that they were a great way of getting a quality session in, but they were hard and generally a means to an end, that being improved fitness and form. With the rise of smart trainers and everything that comes with them, from virtual mountain climbing to intense virtual e-racing, opinions on the latter seem to be a bit more skewed. Some riders, particularly in winter, get stuck into virtual racing to maintain fitness, whilst others shun any sort of virtual world and simply head out in the wet and cold to train. Virtual racing has only grown in recent years; there's a rainbow jersey for it now, and the inaugural UCI Esports World Championship took place back in December 2020. It can also be incredibly lucrative, with big prize pots up for grabs on a regular basis.But does virtual racing really count? It's Indoor Cycling Week at , and the team got together for another editors' roundtable for a healthy exchange of views on the legitimacy of racing indoors. Here are our thoughts, but let us know yours too. Is virtual racing real racing?Is there a treadmill world championship? No, exactly.I could probably stop there, as I think that summarises my point quite well. To me, indoor racing lacks all of the things that make cycling truly competitive. It's a test of fitness, sure (and a difficult one at that; I don't doubt indoor athletes are incredibly strong), but the element of tactics, gameplay, positioning and, to be frank, racing skill is so minimal that it feels very far removed from actual racing.It's also more or less completely useless as a spectator event, which I think is a key element of being a sport – there has to be a degree of entertainment.To me, indoor competition is more akin to the Hyrox world championships or a fitness contest than real bike racing. Challenging and a big achievement for the competitors, yes, but a real sport that the public need particularly pay attention to? Not really. Virtual racing, as Matilda already pointed out, is racing in the way a swim meet is racing. But if rubbing is racing, it's definitely not. You can't throw an elbow, dive the inside of a turn, latch onto another team's lead-out train or use your descending skills to get away from your competition (see Chris Froome/Col de Peyresourde, Matej Mohorič/Sanremo, Marianne Vos/Giro). Real racing takes skill, tactical nous, teamwork and luck – all aspects absent in virtual racing. But if you consider a VO2 max test to be 'real racing', then, sure.Of course, virtual racing is real racing.I haven’t raced a bike for real in a very long time, and there’s no way I’ll go back to it. I wasn’t very good – though I did once win a race – I’m no longer very fit, and even in veterans racing, the variation of ability in the real sport is huge.With online racing you actually race against others of around the same physical ability, which suits me. That said, I’ve only done it once, and then only to test a power meter, but it was short, sweet, incredibly hard, great fun, and Zwift awarded me a new FTP after I came second. And for all those efforts on the road or in any other indoor session, I can never push myself as hard as when there’s the thrill of competition.I’ll certainly give it another go, maybe in the next month or so.No. In much the same way that rowing on an erg machine in the gym doesn’t give you the spray of delicious river water (or sewage, depending on which water company’s area you’re operating in), riding indoors totally fails to offer anything close to the experience of riding and racing outside.Can I take that corner faster, or will the tyres slide? The wind has changed direction. I can’t see; there’s too much grit in my eyes. Indoor racing is sanitised nonsense, and I’d be just as happy having a test to see who has the highest FTP and be done with it, as bike racing without bike handling is just a fitness test.Of course it's real racing. The finish line might be made out of pixels, but if racing on Zwift isn't real racing, then neither is Mario Kart, and I think we all know that it is. Sure, it's not the same as outdoor racing, and it's not a spectator sport. But when I'm being dropped from the lead group on a climb, that feels pretty damn realistic. Can indoor bicycle racing be considered real racing? The 'indoor trainer' remains just that: a fitness tool, not a race machine. Akin to my lovely NordicTrack, which still gets used occasionally, there is no virtual classic cross-country skiing championship, or skimo or even biathlon (can you imagine?). I do think the training apps that allow people to test their skills against each other bring the feel of a peloton, but it is not a real race. Besides, the true definition of 'peloton' – a group moving forward – just doesn't ring true for stationary bikes.Indoor racing is real racing. Indoor racing can be shockingly hard; suffering and pushing as hard as you can whilst sitting on a stationary bike indoors is really tough. Indoor racing and efforts demand a special kind of suffering, and it definitely counts. I see indoor racing sitting off to one side; I’m never going to love it or see it the same way as I see road, or any other kind of real-world racing, but I have respect for the world's best indoor racers; they are putting out incredible numbers and performances indoors, and that takes a certain type of rider and skill set. The effort is very real. Indoor racing also has nuance and tactics that can’t be overlooked; it’s improved as online platforms and technology have developed over time. Indoor racing is legit, but don’t count your indoor kilometres as real ones – they don’t count!The appeal of the bike for me is intrinsically tied to the outdoors, with the unpredictability and sense of discovery of the world around me crucial to my enjoyment of the sport, both as a rider and spectator. That means even track cycling fails to connect in the same way, and virtual racing takes that to a whole other level. Still, while I'm not drawn to virtual racing and struggle to connect with it, I can't dismiss it. The effort and competitive sensations are all real and also I can see how virtual training and racing can be such a valuable tool to close some of the vast chasms in opportunity. The clincher for me is that Australians Jay Vine, Neve Bradbury and Emily Dixon are unquestionably real racers, and they gained their opportunity to enter the pro ranks , despite the geographical hurdles they faced, via a virtual training and racing platform. It's hard to question the validity of a racing medium where talent like that rises to the top. So, yes, virtual racing is real racing, but just please don't make me watch it.If the objective is to get from point A to point B first, then I will call it a race every single time. Yes, virtual racing is real racing. It certainly lacks elements and variables compared to racing on the road, trails, track, etc., but it requires training in strength, endurance, tactics, and skill - even if it is taking place inside of a gaming world. For a lot of athletes, racing is largely a mental battle that is won in the mind first, with drive, focus, confidence, visualisation and the ability to push past limits while under pressure, whether it's on the road or a virtual platform.While there is no treadmill World Championships (yet), there is treadmill racing; ask Eric Min, who caught me right on the finish line for third place in a Zwift race … I'll get him next time we line up on the starting line.

item.title: Severe rainfall and flood warnings issued for central Greece and western Turkey
item.author: Ollie Lewis for MetDesk
item.content:encoded: Turkey has been hit by powerful thunderstorms and a fatal tornado this week with more heavy rain expectedHeavy rain and strong winds will continue to affect parts of south-eastern Europe and Turkey over the next few days, as an area of low pressure in the region has allowed for the formation of powerful thunderstorms. During a particularly intense thunderstorm in Antalya, a coastal city in the south-west of Turkey, the formation of a tornado resulted in the deaths of four construction workers on Tuesday. Authorities in Greece and Turkey have released severe rainfall and flooding warnings, as a further 100-150mm (nearly 4-6in) of rain is expected this week in central Greece and western parts of Turkey, with locally higher totals possible.Travelling eastwards towards south Asia, strong winds and heavy rainfall have swept across the Indian regions of Odisha and Andhra Pradesh as Cyclone Arnab made landfall. With wind gusts in excess of 85mph (140km/h) and rainfall totals in some regions exceeding 200mm, the severe storm has prompted mass evacuations of more than 180,000 people, as well as widespread disruption to energy and transport infrastructure. The cyclone will weaken as it continues to traverse northwards over the coming days, though will continue to deliver heavy rain to parts of northern and central India as it does so.Continue reading...

He was winding down the last 15 minutes of his shift at a vast Google datacentre site in Saint-Ghislain, Belgium, in March, when the call came in. The 34-year-old electrical tester had already worked almost 10 hours, but says such last-minute jobs were normal: “I had no choice. item.title: Game Preview: Knicks at 76ers, October 30, 2026
item.author: Moritz Wollert
item.content:encoded: Last weekend I went to a trading card show with my oldest son here in Germany. Lovely time, great fun. The old man got a nice Jordan, some Ewings and Shaqs, youngster found another Brunson for his collection. At one booth we were flipping through the dollar box as I noticed a rather ugly team logo on the vendor’s sweater. As he politely asked what we were looking for I told him about our love for the Knicks and then couldn’t help myself to make it clear we surely do not look for players of his unlikable squad.The Philly fan laughed, I did too – just some ol’ good natured rubbing. As we discussed the early season I mentioned that he surely had an interesting year ahead of him. “We all know that it’s going to go south somehow”, he chuckled, referring to the bulky knees of his team’s center and other issues his franchise has grown accustomed to. Of course I knew what he was talking about; as you may remember, it was mostly the Knicks who tormented the little brothers from Philly in recent years. Yet I was still amazed at how defeated the nice man sounded regarding his team’s chances.I’m sure you don’t have to look long before you find more obnoxious members of the Sixers fan species, especially after their surprisingly solid start to the season (4 wins, 1 loss). It also includes an opening night win against New York. Of course no Philly fan wants to hear about the asterik of getting the emotionally drained Knicks on Ring Night as a lot of people including their new star player made that game bigger than it actually was.Knicks starting their NBA Cup defense in PhillyAs fate would have it, the Sixers on Friday again have a chance to define themselves against a reigning champion, and again it will be your favorite basketball team. This time the Knicks start their title defense in the much-maligned NBA Cup, that test-tube baby of a basketball competition that clearly had its moments over the years yet feels extremely forced most of the time. No matter if you care about Adam Silver’s money grab or not the game against Philly will surely be an interesting one as it matches the Knicks against a potential playoff opponent and against one of their biggest rivals at the moment.What we saw from the Sixers on Opening Night was a bit of a preview of their early season in general. They played some top-notch defense, helped by the switchability of a motivated LeBron James and the supposedly decent shape Joel Embiid has gotten himself in. Philadelphia has plenty of strong wings, and many of their guys thrive in the passing lanes. It gets them out on the break, as they have a top-5 pace in the NBA right now, and their assist-to-turnover ratio also sits right there with the best teams in the league.Currently, that’s one of the only things they do well on offense, though. Exactly two players from their regular rotation shoot over 45 percent from the field right now; they get no offensive rebounds, and they do not shoot or hit a lot of threes. Even with all their scoring power, their half-court offense has mostly been driven by isolation. Every Philly star takes his turn, mostly with mixed results. Tyrese Maxey clearly has been the best of the brotherly bunch, scoring 28.4 points per game on 46.2 percent shooting.76ers play strong defense yet run a clunky offenseThe bad O and strong D have led to extreme ups and downs early for the newly assembled group, which partly was expected yet might also be a concern going forward. You sure wouldn’t feel that secure if your team got down by 29 against Cleveland in your home opener, then trail Detroit a few nights later by 21 in your only loss just to top it off by going into the 4th quarter down 13 against the Pacers sans Tyrese Haliburton and Ivica Zubac. Begrudgingly, we give them at least some credit for coming back.Either way, the show must and will go on in Philadelphia. Only recently did we see LeBron complain about playing center and Joel Embiid about not playing at all – funny for one of the guys who basically invented the term load management. Jaylen Brown also made headlines talking about his relationship with Jayson Tatum, beef or no beef yet: “Maybe some lamb chops and gravy”. Uh, okay, we’ll chalk it up as just another instance of a guy trying to sound extremely smart and interesting yet doing the exact opposite.For the Knicks it would definitely be smart to not get caught up in all that hoopla. Recently, they have found a much better rhythm on offense, and that will clearly be needed against the physical forces from Philly. Jose Alvarado might be coming back for this one; he is currently listed as a game-time decision. Limiting turnovers will be at a premium as New York does not want to run up and down with the 76ers, especially not on the road. When Nick Nurse tries to hide Embiid on Josh Hart, the Knicks have to punish it. Test the opponent’s communication on the backline with plenty of crisp backdoor cuts, ease the ball-handling pressure for Brunson, and hit your open shots. Sounds easy, I know. In the end, it’s only a game.The vendor at the card show, and we definitely agreed on that. I’m not sure if he’s watching the battle this Friday; maybe he has another show to prepare for. One thing I know, though: I sure would love it if the Knicks gave him a reason to feel a little more defeated.Who: New York Knicks (2-3) at Philadelphia 76ers (4-1)Date: Friday, October 30, 2026Place: Xfinity Mobile Arena, Philadelphia, PAFollow: @ptknicksblog and bsky

item.title: Knicks decline Pacôme Dadiet’s option
item.author: Russell Richardson
item.content:encoded: You’ll recognize the World Champion Pacôme Dadiet from his time spent cheering from the bench or dancing on a parade float. His babyface looks are unchanged since his NBA debut—much like his skills.In a (not so) surprising move, the Knicks have declined to pick up the option for this important practice player. Scoopman Shams Charania reports that the Knicks “plan to decline Pacome Dadiet’s fourth-year option worth $5.37 million, sources tell ESPN.”This money move will free up a little cap space for Leon Rose as he crunches contract numbers for Karl-Anthony Towns, Josh Hart, and presumably Miles McBride and Tyler Kolek. The Frenchman will be an unrestricted free agent next summer.Dadiet appeared in 18 games as a rookie, 29 as a sophomore, and for one minute of one game in the current campaign. He also played two seasons in the G League with the Westchester club. Late in his second season there, he delivered multiple 25–32-point games, including a 32-point outing with five boards, four dimes, two thefts, and a block.Although he seemed to be improving in the minor leagues, he hasn’t shown it in his limited appearances at MSG. The best young NBA players demonstrate growth from year to year, with crisper floor movement, shot refinement, physical development, and increased BB IQ. Not so with Pac-Man. The barely 21-year-old will leave an important legacy in New York, however, even if this is indeed his final season with the club.When selected with the 25th pick in the 2024 NBA Draft, Dadiet agreed to a four-year rookie-scale deal worth about $13.01 million rather than the more typical maximum scale amount near $13.9 million. First-round rookies can sign for as little as 80% or as much as 120% of the slotted amount. Dadiet took the minimum 80% for 2024-25, a first-year salary of roughly $1.81 million instead of around $2.71 million.This created about $904,000 in extra flexibility under the 2024-25 second-apron hard cap. The Knicks also paid an $850,000 buyout to free him from his German club (Ratiopharm Ulm), but that overseas buyout did not count against the NBA salary cap.Without that discount, the subsequent trade for Karl-Anthony Towns (which sent Julius Randle, Donte DiVincenzo, and other pieces to Minnesota, with Charlotte involved for salary matching) would have nudged New York over the second apron. The Towns acquisition as structured would have been impossible, at least in that form.Later seasons of Dadiet’s deal moved closer to (or above) standard scale, but by originally “taking less,” he helped facilitate the acquisition of KAT, who helped deliver a championship to the city two years later.The new season is still young—and so is he—but Dads already has a ring and some serious bragging rights. If the ride ends after this season, he’s got plenty to be proud of.

item.title: Who can compete as a gravel pro in Unbound? Organisers of Life Time Grand Prix establish new 'Pro Number' qualification process
item.author: jackie.tyson@futurenet.com (Jackie Tyson)
item.content:encoded: A 'LT Pro Number' will now be required for riders to compete in the professional category across Life Time events, from the Sea Otter Qualifier in April to individual events that are part of the Life Time Grand Prix off-road series, including Unbound Gravel 200. Many athletes will receive automatic approval for a LT Pro Number, based on past results in Life Time pro events, the Life Time Grand Prix series, as well as status with national and world championships, related to mountain bike or gravel. Life Time, which owns and operates more than 195 athletic country clubs across the U.S. and Canada as well as endurance, cycling and running events, also outlined factors considered by a selection committee which will look at results in age groups and races outside the Life Time family.Safety was the driving factor to implement the new criteria, based on results as well as past experience. The process was also seen as a way to "further professionalize the sport", as the Life Time Grand Prix enters a sixth season in 2027.“We love that our events bring together athletes of all ages and abilities, and create opportunities for people to challenge themselves. At the same time, mass participant events like Unbound and Leadville are fast and can be tightly packed, particularly at the front of the field. "Establishing clear, performance-based criteria for the Pro start helps ensure riders competing at the front have demonstrated the experience and ability to race safely at that level, while providing a transparent pathway for athletes to earn their place," Michelle Duffy, director of the Life Time Grand Prix, stated in the announcement on Thursday.Concerns about the scramble for positioning at the front of the elite fields had been raised in the past by athletes themselves, especially at the two most demanding races - Unbound Gravel 200 and Leadville Trail 100 MTB. During the Unbound Gravel 200 two years ago, there were several crashes involving less-experienced riders with Grand Prix contenders in the first six miles. The new protocols will help ensure riders have "demonstrated the ability and experience to compete at the front of the fast-race starts" before they line up, according to Life Time.This new vetting system requires each rider to register online, with one approval covering all events for one year. The LT Pro Number does not guarantee entry, with registration or lottery request still required. For LT Pro Qualifier races, such as Sea Otter Classic Gravel 60, Sea Otter Classic Fuego XL, Lutsen 99er and four other events, the races are open to all participants and no LT Pro Number is required. With good results, a rider can earn an LT Pro Number in order to complete registration for LT Pro events.Life Time noted that the entire process would be transparent, with all cut off times and qualifying places posted publicly for athletes to track.The road season might be at an end, but Cyclingnews isn't slowing down. item.title: Praying for the healthy Knicks as we approach Día de Muertos
item.author: Antonio Losada
item.content:encoded: It’s not even Halloween, the NBA season is barely a week old, but the injury report already looks like something you’d expect to read in April. Here in Mexico City, I can relate. You can feel in the air, both figuratively and literally. We’re just days — hours, if you push it — away from one of the biggest festivities in the country to take place this weekend. No need to explain what we celebrate, trying to bring back those who left us in the past to start just another chapter away from the land. If only for a little .Meanwhile, in the NBA, it looks like stars are playing a very solid role in a performance mimicking this weekend’s celebrations. It’s not a few, but , who have already undergone surgery and be placed on the shelves for months on end, if not the whole year, outright.Meanwhile, the New York Knicks are doing something that is starting to feel illegal, some sort of subterfuge competitive advantage in itself.Being healthy. .Now compare that with the rest of the league, where approximately 15 percent of players (s/o Keerthika!) were dealing with injuries or illnesses yesterday afternoon. Eleven former All-Stars were already expected to miss several weeks or longer just eight days into the season.The NBA injury report is a hot Obviously, the most concerning situation might be in Oklahoma City, where Jalen Williams underwent surgery to repair a fractured left fibula and reconstruct ankle ligaments following a fracture-dislocation and will only be by the team when the regular season . Gone for good, in other words. Descanse en paz, bendito. His teammate Cason Wallace also needs surgery after tearing the labrum in his left shoulder, and both will miss a hellaciously long time.Minnesota’s Anthony Edwards underwent arthroscopic surgery on his right knee and could miss two months. Utah’s Jaren Jackson Jr. tore the MCL in his right knee and faces a six-to-eight-week absence. Indiana’s Tyrese Haliburton, already coming off a season lost to an Achilles injury, will miss at least two weeks with a hamstring strain. Orlando’s Paolo Banchero faces four to six weeks out with a high ankle sprain, while Toronto’s Kawhi Leonard is expected to miss multiple weeks because of swelling in his left knee. Elsewhere, Golden State is without Jimmy Butler III until potentially January or February, while Kristaps Porzingis remains away indefinitely with ongoing health concerns. Sacramento’s Ben Simmons and former Knickerbocker Ariel Hukporti suffered Achilles ruptures, and Washington’s Jamir Watkins is recovering from ACL surgery.Hay más almas que cempasúchil en el sendero.Somehow, the Knicks have avoided all of thisAs Stefan Bondy of the New York Post noted, every member of the Knicks’ starting five reached the 65-game threshold in both 2024-25 and 2025-26. Jalen Brunson, Mikal Bridges, Josh Hart, OG Anunoby, and Karl-Anthony Towns have provided a level of continuity that most teams can only dream about. Bridges hasn’t missed an NBA game in his career even though seemingly everybody wants him hitting the pine for a start, with his streak reaching 643 consecutive appearances on Wednesday. Towns and Anunoby, meanwhile, arrived in New York with considerable injury histories but have remained remarkably durable.Per Bondy, the Knicks’ starting five led the NBA with 940 minutes together in 2024-25, finished second with 541 last season, and ranked first again through four games this year.Around the NBA: Oct. 29 injury reportESPN listed across on its injury report, with the San Antonio Spurs and the Memphis Grizzlies, , escaping .Here’s the list.
